findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Biometric Information Exclusion (manufacturer exposure)
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirements were provided for this audit. Finding is policy-side only.
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement EPL 170 — Biometric Information Exclusion (referenced on Pg. 8 of the Renewal Certificate).
findings.gap_description: Form EPL 170 excludes claims arising out of the collection, use, storage, or disclosure of biometric identifiers and biometric information. There is no other policy in the disclosed Precision Aero program (no Cyber/Privacy policy, no D&O, no MPL) that would respond to a biometric-privacy class action. Biometric privacy statutes — Illinois BIPA, Texas CUBI, Washington H.B. 1493, and now California, New York, and Colorado equivalents — provide statutory damages of $1,000–$5,000 per violation, per individual, per incident. Single-employer settlements have exceeded $50M (e.g., White Castle, BNSF). For a manufacturing operation that may use biometric time clocks, fingerprint or hand-geometry plant access, or facial recognition at security checkpoints, this is a coverage void with no fallback policy.
findings.plain_english: If Precision Aero uses any kind of fingerprint, palm, or face scan to clock in employees or control plant access — even if you bought it from a vendor and don't think of it as 'biometric' — there is a class-action lawsuit category that is exploding nationwide, and your EPLI policy specifically excludes it. There is no other policy in the program that would pick it up. A single bad disclosure or consent practice can cost millions, and you would write the check personally. We need to confirm whether you use any biometric identification on the production floor, and if you do, get a Cyber/Privacy policy with affirmative biometric coverage (or buy back the EPLI exclusion) before the next BIPA-style law lands in Arizona.
findings.recommendation: 1) Confirm at intake whether Precision Aero uses any biometric employee identification (time clocks, badge readers with biometric backup, facial recognition cameras, fingerprint logins on shop-floor terminals). 2) If yes, market a standalone Cyber/Privacy policy with affirmative biometric coverage (or pursue a manuscripted EPL 170 buy-back with USLI). 3) Implement BIPA-compliant written consent and retention/destruction policy regardless of state — most carriers will require this as a condition of binding biometric coverage.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through how an employee on the production floor clocks in and out of a shift — is it a card swipe, a code, or a fingerprint or hand scan?
Have you or your HR team heard of BIPA, the Illinois biometric law? What about Texas CUBI? They've been generating $50M+ class-action settlements against manufacturers.
If a former employee filed a class action tomorrow alleging you collected their fingerprint without proper written consent, do you know which insurance policy would defend you?
What's your written employee-consent and data-retention policy for any fingerprint, face, or hand-scan data your access systems collect?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Retroactive Date / Prior Acts
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement EPL-148 — Retroactive Date Endorsement: 'Section II Full Prior Acts Coverage Provision is deleted and replaced with a retroactive date of 11/30/2022.' (Pg. 11)
findings.gap_description: EPLI is a claims-made coverage form. EPL-148 deletes the Full Prior Acts Coverage Provision and substitutes a retroactive date of 11/30/2022. As of the 11/30/2023 inception this provides only one year of prior-acts coverage. Any wrongful employment act committed prior to 11/30/2022 is permanently uncovered, even if the EEOC charge or lawsuit is filed during this policy period. Employment claims routinely arise long after the underlying conduct (constructive discharge claims, retaliation tied to old protected activity, harassment claims years after the fact). If Precision Aero had EPLI in prior years, the retroactive date should match the earliest continuous EPLI inception, not be cut to one year — that is a material erosion of coverage at renewal.
findings.plain_english: Employment lawsuits don't always show up right after the event — a manager who fired someone in 2021 can still get hit with a charge in 2024. This policy says: anything that actually happened before November 2022 is not covered, no matter when the lawsuit shows up. If you've had EPLI in place for years, your retroactive date should go back to your very first EPLI policy, not just one year. Cutting it to one year is the same as throwing away most of the value you've already paid for.
findings.recommendation: 1) Pull the prior EPLI declarations to confirm continuous EPLI inception date. 2) If continuous coverage exists, demand USLI delete EPL-148 and reinstate Full Prior Acts (a renewal carrier should match the prior retro). 3) If this is genuinely the first EPLI policy, build a multi-year retro plan: full prior acts at next renewal, with documentation of continuity going forward. 4) If USLI refuses, market the renewal — most standard EPLI carriers offer Full Prior Acts at competitive terms.
discoveryQuestions: How long has Precision Aero had EPLI coverage in place — is this your first year, or have you been buying it continuously?
If you have prior EPLI policies, what was the retroactive date on those policies? Did anyone walk you through what changed at this renewal?
Are you aware that an employee terminated in 2021 could still file an EEOC charge in 2024 — and that your current policy would not cover the underlying conduct?
When the renewal came in with a new retroactive date, did the carrier or your prior broker explain that you were giving up coverage you previously had?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Limit Adequacy ($1M Aggregate)
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Each Claim Limit: $1,000,000. Aggregate Limit: $1,000,000. Retention Each Claim: $25,000. (Pg. 9)
findings.gap_description: Both Each-Claim and Aggregate limits are set at $1,000,000. The aggregate is shared across all claims in the policy year. EPLI defense alone for a single multi-plaintiff discrimination, harassment, or wrongful-termination matter can exceed $500K–$1M, especially in California or with a regulatory overlay. Defense-cost-vs.-limit erosion (whether defense erodes the limit or sits outside it) is not visible from the renewal certificate text and must be confirmed against the EPL-J base form — most EPLI policies have defense INSIDE the limit, meaning a single moderately serious matter could exhaust the $1M aggregate and leave Precision Aero with zero coverage for the rest of the policy year.
findings.plain_english: $1M sounds like a lot, but in employment law it isn't. Defense costs alone on a class-style discrimination case can easily eat half a million dollars before you even talk about a settlement. And the $1M is shared across every claim that hits in the year — so one ugly claim in March and you're naked for the rest of the year. For a manufacturer with hourly employees, $2M to $5M is more appropriate, and the cost difference is usually small relative to the additional protection.
findings.recommendation: 1) Quote $2M and $5M aggregate options at next renewal — premium spread is usually modest. 2) Confirm whether defense costs are inside or outside the limit (verify against EPL-J coverage form). If defense is inside the limit, that pushes the case for higher aggregate even harder. 3) Benchmark against employee headcount and state mix — California/New York/Illinois exposure justifies more than a Midwest manufacturer with the same headcount.
discoveryQuestions: Roughly how many employees does Precision Aero have, and what's the state mix — any California, New York, or Illinois locations?
Have you seen what defense alone costs on a multi-plaintiff harassment or discrimination case? Six figures is normal before anyone settles anything.
If a single class-action wage-and-hour case ate the entire $1M in March, how would you feel about being uninsured for any other employee dispute through November?
When was the last time anyone benchmarked your EPLI limit against your peer group — manufacturers your size and shape?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Wage & Hour Sublimit (FLSA)
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement EPL-162 — Fair Labor Standards Act Sub-Limit Endorsement (referenced Pg. 8). Sublimit dollar amount not visible on renewal certificate.
findings.gap_description: EPL-162 sublimits FLSA / wage-and-hour exposure (defense costs and possibly indemnity) below the $1M aggregate. The dollar amount of the sublimit is not stated on the renewal certificate. Wage & hour is the highest-frequency, highest-severity employment exposure for most hourly-workforce employers — misclassification, off-the-clock work, meal-and-rest break violations, and PAGA-style claims (in CA) regularly produce six- and seven-figure settlements. Sublimits below $250K defense are inadequate for a manufacturer with production-floor employees.
findings.plain_english: The biggest, most common employment lawsuit in America right now isn't sexual harassment — it's wage and hour: 'you didn't pay me overtime,' 'you made me work through lunch,' 'you misclassified me as exempt.' Your policy carves out a special, smaller bucket of money for those claims, and we don't even know how big that bucket is yet. For a manufacturer with hourly workers, this is the lawsuit that's actually coming.
findings.recommendation: 1) Pull the EPL-162 endorsement form text immediately to determine the sublimit dollar amount. 2) If sublimit is below $250K defense-only, push USLI to increase it or market alternative carriers (Hartford, Travelers, Chubb offer higher wage-and-hour sublimits or full-limit defense). 3) Implement defensive measures: pay-practice audit, exempt-classification review, time-records and break-policy compliance — most carriers offer free risk-management consultations on this exposure.
discoveryQuestions: How are your production employees paid — hourly with overtime, or do you have anyone classified as exempt who's borderline?
When was the last time anyone audited whether your supervisors are correctly classified as exempt under the new federal salary threshold?
What's your meal-and-break policy on the shop floor, and how is it documented? Could a former employee credibly claim they worked through lunch?
If a wage-and-hour collective action hit tomorrow naming you and ten other hourly workers, do you know what dollar amount of defense your policy actually pays before you're on your own?

findings.requirement_type: Renewal Certificate Only — Full Policy Text Not Available for Audit
findings.policy_quote: Document analyzed is the Renewal Certificate plus marketing inserts. Forms EPL-J (base coverage form), EPL-AZ (Arizona Amendatory), EPL-167 (Amended Definition of Loss), EPL-169 (Amended Notice/Claim Provisions), and the Policy Jacket are referenced but not included.
findings.gap_description: The audit was performed against a Renewal Certificate, not the full bound policy. Material coverage terms cannot be verified without the full forms: (a) cancellation and nonrenewal notice period, (b) hammer clause / consent-to-settle structure, (c) whether defense costs erode the $1M limit or sit outside, (d) definition of 'Employee' (W-2 only? leased workers? 1099 contractors? volunteers?), (e) third-party harassment coverage scope, (f) punitive damages treatment (covered, excluded, or 'where insurable by law'), (g) the dollar sublimit on EPL-162 wage & hour, (h) exactly what EPL-167 changes about the Loss definition (front pay, back pay, liquidated damages, equitable relief), (i) what EPL-169 changes about notice and circumstance reporting triggers, (j) Arizona-specific amendatory effects.
findings.plain_english: We're auditing from a summary, not the actual policy. Several of the answers a CFO needs to know — like 'if I get sued, do I get to pick my lawyer?' or 'how much notice does the carrier have to give before they cancel?' — are written in pages we haven't seen. Before we tell you the program is solid, we need the full policy in hand.
findings.recommendation: Request the complete bound policy from USLI — including the EPL-J coverage form, EPL-AZ Arizona Amendatory, all numbered endorsements (EPL-148, EPL-162, EPL-167, EPL-169, EPL 170), and the Policy Jacket. Re-run the audit against the full document before issuing the final findings report.

findings.requirement_type: General — 90-Day Notice of Cancellation
findings.policy_quote: Cancellation notice period not visible in renewal certificate text. Governed by EPL-AZ Arizona State Amendatory Endorsement and policy jacket — neither included in document provided.
findings.gap_description: Broker benchmark is 90-day notice of cancellation (60-day floor). Standard USLI EPLI cancellation provisions, modified by Arizona state amendatory, typically run 30–60 days for nonpayment and 60 days for other reasons — but the actual provision cannot be read from the renewal certificate. If the policy provides less than 60 days' for-cause notice, that is a finding worth flagging at next renewal.
findings.plain_english: How much warning your carrier has to give before they cancel you matters a lot — especially mid-policy. The standard we want for our clients is 90 days. We can't see what your policy actually says from this document, so we need to verify against the full policy form.
findings.recommendation: Pull the cancellation provision from the EPL-J base form and the EPL-AZ Arizona Amendatory. Document the for-cause and nonpayment notice days. If less than 60 days for-cause, request a Designated Entity / extended-notice endorsement at next renewal — most EPLI carriers will accommodate at no charge.

findings.requirement_type: General — Unintentional Errors and Omissions Giveback
findings.policy_quote: No Unintentional E&O endorsement listed in the form schedule (Pg. 8). Standard USLI EPLI form may include comparable language embedded in EPL-J coverage form definitions — text not available.
findings.gap_description: Unintentional E&O givebacks are most common on GL/Property/Auto. On EPLI, the analogous concern is whether innocent failure to disclose material facts at application or renewal voids coverage. Without the EPL-J coverage form text we cannot confirm whether USLI's EPLI form provides an innocent-insureds / innocent-misrepresentation severability provision. Worth confirming.
findings.plain_english: Sometimes a policy says 'if anyone in your company gave us wrong information, we can void everything.' A good policy carves out the innocent people. We need to read the full form to confirm USLI gives you that protection.
findings.recommendation: Verify EPL-J base form for an innocent-insureds severability provision and an innocent-misrepresentation clause. If absent, request endorsement at next renewal.

findings.requirement_type: General — Named Insureds Across Program
findings.policy_quote: Named Insured: Precision Aero, Inc. (Pg. 9). No Additional Named Insureds; no Broad Form Named Insured endorsement.
findings.gap_description: EPLI Named Insured is Precision Aero, Inc. — Inc. entity type, single named entity. No subsidiaries, holding companies, real-estate LLCs, or 401(k) plan are scheduled. Without visibility into the rest of the program (no other policies were provided in this audit data), we cannot confirm cross-policy NI consistency. If Precision Aero has any related entities (a holding company, a real-estate LLC that owns the plant, a separately-incorporated benefits trust), they need to be either scheduled as Additional Named Insureds or covered by a Broad Form Named Insured endorsement.
findings.plain_english: The policy only protects 'Precision Aero, Inc.' — the exact corporate name. If there's a holding company, a separate LLC that owns the building, or a 401(k) trust on the org chart, an employment claim against any of those entities might not be covered. Common gap, easy fix.
findings.recommendation: 1) Obtain Precision Aero org chart at intake. 2) Schedule every operating, holding, and benefit-plan entity as an Additional Named Insured on EPLI (USLI typically charges nothing for this). 3) Confirm consistency across all policies in the program — a Named Insured present on Auto/GL but missing from EPLI/Umbrella is the most common gap.

findings.requirement_type: General — Notice and Knowledge Endorsement
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement EPL-169 — Amended Notice/Claim and Circumstance Reporting Provisions (Pg. 8). Form text not in renewal certificate.
findings.gap_description: EPL-169 modifies notice and circumstance reporting. Without the form text we cannot determine whether (a) notice/knowledge is limited to officers/HR director/risk manager — protecting the company from imputation of knowledge by a low-level supervisor — or (b) the endorsement tightens reporting triggers in a way that increases late-notice forfeiture risk. Best practice is officer-limited notice.
findings.plain_english: If a shift supervisor knows about a harassment complaint and doesn't tell HR, does that count as 'the company knew' for purposes of this policy? You want the answer to be 'no — only officers and HR knowing counts.' We need to read the actual endorsement to confirm.
findings.recommendation: Pull EPL-169 form text. Confirm notice/knowledge is limited to officers, HR director, or risk manager. If the endorsement instead tightens reporting in a way unfavorable to the insured, push back at next renewal.

findings.requirement_type: General — Waiver of Subrogation
findings.gap_description: Waiver of Subrogation is generally not applicable to EPLI policies — employment claims are first-party employee-vs.-employer matters with no third-party recovery rights for the carrier to waive. No finding warranted unless a specific contract requires WoS on EPLI.
findings.plain_english: Waiver of subrogation isn't really a thing on EPLI — there's nobody for the insurance company to chase after they pay an employment claim. Non-issue here.
findings.recommendation: No action required for EPLI. Confirm WoS applies as required by contract on GL, Auto, WC, Property, and Inland Marine policies (none of which are present in the disclosed program for review).

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Defense Costs Erosion of Limit
findings.policy_quote: Renewal Certificate notes: 'Defense Costs shall be applied against the Retention.' (Pg. 9). Whether defense costs also erode the $1M limit is not stated on the certificate.
findings.gap_description: EPLI policies typically have defense INSIDE the limit (defense costs reduce the available limit dollar-for-dollar). The renewal certificate confirms defense erodes the retention but does not state whether it also erodes the limit. Most USLI EPLI forms put defense inside the limit. If confirmed, this strengthens the case for higher limits — see Finding #003.
findings.plain_english: On most EPLI policies, every dollar your lawyer spends defending you is a dollar that comes out of your $1M coverage bucket. If this is one of those policies — and it probably is — it's another reason the $1M is too thin.
findings.recommendation: Verify defense-cost treatment in EPL-J coverage form. If defense is inside the limit (most likely), incorporate that into the limit-adequacy recommendation in Finding #003. If defense is outside the limit, that is a meaningfully better policy than typical EPLI — credit the carrier.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Definition of 'Employee' (Temps, Leased Workers, 1099)
findings.policy_quote: Definition of 'Employee' lives in EPL-J base coverage form — text not available in renewal certificate.
findings.gap_description: Whether the EPLI policy's definition of 'Employee' covers temporary workers, leased workers from a staffing agency, seasonal labor, and properly-classified 1099 contractors is material for a manufacturer that almost certainly uses temp/contract labor at peak production. If the definition is W-2-only and a temp brings a harassment claim, the matter could be uncovered. Also relevant: third-party harassment coverage (claims by non-employees alleging harassment by Precision Aero personnel) — many manufacturers face these from delivery drivers and customer reps.
findings.plain_english: If you bring in temps from Manpower or similar agencies during busy season, and one of them files a harassment claim, does your policy cover the company defending that claim? Sometimes yes, sometimes no — depends on how 'employee' is written in the form. Worth nailing down.
findings.recommendation: Pull EPL-J definition of 'Employee.' Confirm coverage scope for: (a) full-time W-2, (b) part-time, (c) leased workers from staffing agencies, (d) temporary workers, (e) seasonal workers, (f) properly-classified independent contractors performing services for the insured. Confirm presence of third-party (non-employee) harassment coverage.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Hammer Clause / Consent to Settle
findings.policy_quote: Hammer clause / consent-to-settle structure lives in EPL-J base coverage form — text not available.
findings.gap_description: EPLI hammer clauses range from harsh (100% of additional defense and indemnity if insured refuses settlement) to soft (50/50 or 70/30 split) to advisory (no penalty, but carrier loses excess defense obligation). Reputational employment matters — a wrongful-termination case from a long-tenured employee, or a harassment matter that could go public — frequently involve the insured wanting to fight what the carrier wants to settle. The hammer clause structure dictates how much that costs the insured.
findings.plain_english: If your carrier wants to write a check to settle a case but you'd rather fight on principle, what does it cost you? On the worst policies, you eat 100% of everything from that point forward. On better policies, you split it 50/50. We need to read what yours says.
findings.recommendation: Pull EPL-J hammer clause language. If 100% hammer, push for a soft hammer (50/50 or 70/30) at next renewal — common concession for accounts of any size with a clean loss history.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Carrier Financial Strength
findings.policy_quote: Carrier: United States Liability Insurance Company (USLI), a Berkshire Hathaway subsidiary. AM Best rating: A++ (Superior). (Pg. 9)
findings.gap_description: Carrier is admitted, A++ Best rated, and a Berkshire Hathaway subsidiary. No financial-strength concern.
findings.plain_english: USLI is owned by Berkshire Hathaway and rated A++ — about as strong as carriers get. If they have to pay a claim, they will pay it. No issue here.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Document A++ rating in renewal file.

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No General Liability Policy
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No CGL policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: No Commercial General Liability policy was disclosed in the program data provided for this audit. A manufacturer without CGL has no insurance for: (a) bodily injury and property damage to third parties (visitors injured at the plant, products causing third-party injury, premises liability), (b) products/completed operations exposure (a defective component injuring an end user — catastrophic for an aerospace component manufacturer), (c) personal and advertising injury, (d) any contractual indemnity obligations to upstream OEMs or suppliers, (e) Additional Insured status on certificates required by virtually every commercial customer. This is a business-ending exposure for any manufacturer and especially for one in aerospace.
findings.plain_english: If there is no General Liability policy in the program, this is the single biggest red flag in the entire audit. No GL means: a customer slips at your facility — you pay. A defective part you machined causes an aerospace incident downstream — you pay. Every customer who asks for a certificate of insurance gets nothing. We need to confirm immediately whether a CGL policy exists that wasn't in the file, or get one bound today.
findings.recommendation: URGENT: Confirm whether a CGL policy exists outside the documents provided. If no CGL is in force, bind a Commercial General Liability policy immediately — minimum $1M/$2M occurrence/aggregate plus a $5M/$10M Umbrella, with manufacturers/products coverage, blanket Additional Insured (CG 20 10 + CG 20 37), Waiver of Subrogation (CG 24 04), and Primary & Noncontributory wording.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through your insurance program — do you have a General Liability policy somewhere I haven't seen yet, or is EPLI really the only liability coverage you're carrying?
When customers ask for a certificate of insurance naming them as additional insured, what document do you send them today?
If a part you machined caused an aircraft incident downstream, who do you think pays the lawsuit — you or the airframe OEM?
What does your largest customer's contract require you to carry in terms of GL, products, and additional insured status?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Workers' Compensation Policy
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No Workers' Compensation policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: No Workers' Compensation policy was disclosed for a manufacturer with employees. Workers' Compensation is statutorily required in 49 of 50 states for any employer with employees (Texas the only exception, and even there most employers carry it). A manufacturing operation with shop-floor workers running CNC machines, presses, and assembly equipment has elevated frequency-and-severity injury exposure. Without WC: (a) every workplace injury is a direct hit to corporate cash, (b) statutory penalties for failure to carry WC range from per-day fines to criminal liability for owners, (c) injured workers can sue in tort outside the workers'-comp exclusive remedy — meaning unlimited liability for what would otherwise be a capped statutory claim.
findings.plain_english: If you have employees and no Workers' Comp policy, you are violating state law in nearly every state — and you're personally on the hook for every shop-floor injury. A single serious press or CNC accident in a machine shop can run into seven figures, and your CFO writes that check from operating cash. We need to confirm a WC policy exists and just wasn't in this file.
findings.recommendation: URGENT: Confirm whether a Workers' Compensation policy exists outside the documents provided. If not in force, bind WC immediately in every state of operation — statutory limits, $1M/$1M/$1M Employers' Liability minimum (higher to support Umbrella attachment), Alternate Employer endorsement if any leased labor, blanket Waiver of Subrogation. Verify experience-mod accuracy and All-States Endorsement coverage.
discoveryQuestions: Confirm for me — do you have a Workers' Compensation policy somewhere outside this file, and which carrier is it with?
What states does Precision Aero have employees in, and is every state listed on Item 3.A of your WC policy?
What's your current experience modification factor, and what's the trend over the last three years?
When was the last time a broker walked the shop floor with you to compare actual operations against the class codes on the WC policy?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Commercial Auto Policy
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No Commercial Auto policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: No Commercial Auto policy in the disclosed program. Even manufacturers without an owned fleet have auto exposure: (a) any owned vehicle (delivery, parts runner, sales rep car, owner's company vehicle), (b) hired auto exposure (rental cars on business trips), (c) non-owned auto exposure (employees running errands in personal vehicles for the company — Costco run, post office, customer pickup). Without any auto policy, Hired & Non-Owned Auto must at minimum be endorsed onto the GL — and there is no GL in the program either.
findings.plain_english: Even if you don't own a single truck, the moment an employee drives their own car on company business — even just to pick up lunch for a client meeting — and gets into a serious accident, the company gets sued. With no Auto policy and no GL with HNOA endorsed on, every one of those trips is uninsured.
findings.recommendation: 1) Determine fleet status — owned vehicles, leased vehicles, employee-owned-used-for-business. 2) If owned/leased fleet: bind Business Auto with $1M CSL minimum, Symbol 1 (any auto), HNOA included, blanket AI/WoS, Drive Other Car for executive officers. 3) If no owned fleet: at minimum endorse HNOA onto a CGL policy (which also needs to be put in force per Finding #015).
discoveryQuestions: Does Precision Aero own any vehicles — a parts runner, a sales rep car, a forklift on the road, anything titled to the company?
When an employee drives their own car on company business — picking up parts, dropping off a quote, running to the airport for a customer visit — whose insurance pays if they hit someone?
If a delivery driver damaged a customer's loading dock unloading product, do you know which policy responds?
Have you ever rented a car on a business trip and used your personal credit card's coverage instead of the company's? How would a serious injury claim from that rental be handled?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Umbrella / Excess Liability
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No Umbrella/Excess policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: No Umbrella in the disclosed program. For an aerospace component manufacturer, $1M primary limits on GL/Auto/WC are inadequate for a serious incident — a products-liability claim involving downed aircraft, a multi-vehicle highway accident, or a catastrophic shop-floor injury can reach eight figures. Without an Umbrella, the program ceiling is the underlying primary limit, leaving the company directly exposed for everything above $1M.
findings.plain_english: For an aerospace parts manufacturer, $1M of liability protection is dinner money. A single bad parts-related incident on an aircraft, or a fatality on the shop floor, can put a $10M+ judgment on the table. Without an umbrella, every dollar above the underlying limit comes out of the company's pocket — and could end the company.
findings.recommendation: Bind Commercial Umbrella with minimum $5M/$5M limits (target $10M for an aerospace manufacturer), follow-form over GL/Auto/Employers' Liability, schedule of underlying with all policies listed, blanket Additional Insured follow-form, blanket Waiver of Subrogation follow-form, defense outside limits where available, no broader exclusions than underlying.
discoveryQuestions: If a part you manufactured was implicated in an aviation incident with multiple fatalities, where do you think the lawsuit ends — at $1M, or somewhere with a lot more zeros?
What do your largest customers' contracts require for total combined liability limits — primary plus umbrella?
When was the last time you stress-tested your insurance program against a worst-case scenario rather than an average one?
If a $5M judgment landed tomorrow, does Precision Aero have $4M of operating cash sitting around to cover the gap above your primary?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Property / Inland Marine
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No Property or Inland Marine policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: No Property or Inland Marine policy in the disclosed program. An aerospace manufacturer typically has significant exposure in: (a) building (owned or as a tenant with improvements & betterments), (b) machinery and equipment (CNC machines run six- and seven-figures each), (c) raw materials and finished goods inventory (often customer-owned and subject to bailee liability), (d) business income / extended period of indemnity (post-loss revenue gap), (e) property in transit, (f) computer equipment and CAD/CAM systems, (g) potential equipment breakdown / mechanical failure exposure.
findings.plain_english: If a fire takes out the shop tomorrow, who pays for the new CNC machines, the raw titanium inventory, and the lost revenue while you rebuild? Without a property policy, you do — out of pocket. For a precision-machining shop, the equipment alone can be a multi-million-dollar replacement.
findings.recommendation: Bind Commercial Property + Business Income on a special-form, replacement-cost basis, with adequate equipment-breakdown coverage and 12-month minimum BI/EPI. Add Inland Marine for property-in-transit and customer-owned property bailee coverage if Precision Aero handles consigned inventory. Confirm any mortgagee or lessor requirements.
discoveryQuestions: If the shop burned down on Saturday night, what's the dollar figure to replace every CNC machine, every press, every measuring station, and every piece of finished inventory inside?

How many months of revenue would Precision Aero lose while finding a new building, replacing the equipment, and getting back into production — and how many months of payroll could you carry without that revenue?
Do you ever hold customer-owned material on the shop floor — consigned titanium, customer tooling, a part in for rework? Whose insurance covers it while it's in your possession?
Who's the mortgage holder or landlord, and what does the loan or lease require you to carry in terms of property limits and named-mortgagee/loss-payee status?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Cyber Liability Policy
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No Cyber Liability policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: No Cyber/Privacy policy in the disclosed program. Manufacturers — and aerospace manufacturers especially — are top ransomware targets: (a) operational technology (PLCs, CNC controllers, MES systems) is brittle and high-value, (b) ransomware shutdown of production is more expensive per day than data-breach class actions, (c) aerospace customers (Boeing, Lockheed, Tier-1 suppliers) increasingly require CMMC compliance and breach-notification cooperation under DFARS 252.204-7012, (d) biometric privacy claims (see Finding #001) need a cyber/privacy policy as the only home in the program. Without Cyber, Precision Aero has no first-party coverage for ransom payment, business interruption from a cyber event, breach response (forensics, notification, credit monitoring), and no third-party coverage for regulatory defense or class actions.
findings.plain_english: Aerospace manufacturers are sitting in the bullseye for ransomware. The bad guys know your shop floor stops cold if their CNC controllers are encrypted, and they price the ransom accordingly. Without cyber insurance, you're paying the ransom — or paying for the downtime — out of pocket. And on top of that, you've got a biometric exclusion on EPLI with no other policy in the program that covers it. We need cyber.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Cyber/Privacy policy with: (a) $2M-$5M aggregate limit minimum, (b) ransomware/extortion at full limit (not sublimited), (c) business interruption with 12-hour waiting period and 12-month indemnity, (d) dependent business interruption (vendor outage), (e) breach response panel including forensics and notification, (f) regulatory defense, (g) social engineering / wire transfer fraud, (h) AFFIRMATIVE biometric privacy coverage to backstop the EPL 170 exclusion, (i) DFARS / CMMC compliance assistance if working defense aerospace.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through what happens if you arrive Monday morning and every controller on the shop floor is locked with a ransom note — who do you call first, and what does that day cost you?
Do you have any defense-aerospace customers, and are you subject to CMMC or DFARS 252.204-7012 cybersecurity requirements?
Has anyone in your office ever clicked a link they shouldn't have, or has Precision Aero ever wired money based on a spoofed email request?

Given that your EPLI excludes biometric claims and you may use fingerprint time clocks, do you understand that without Cyber there is literally no policy in your program that responds to a BIPA-style class action?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Directors & Officers / Management Liability
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No D&O / Management Liability policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: No D&O policy in the disclosed program. Even private companies face D&O exposure: (a) shareholder/investor disputes, (b) creditor claims on insolvency, (c) regulatory investigations (OSHA, EPA, FAA for aerospace), (d) M&A representations and warranties claims, (e) personal asset exposure for directors and officers in any of the above. Private-company D&O is typically bundled with EPLI, Crime, and Fiduciary as a Management Liability package — the EPLI here is monoline and not part of a package.
findings.plain_english: Right now, if a regulator opens an investigation, or a shareholder files a derivative lawsuit, or a creditor goes after the owners personally, the company's officers and directors are paying for their own defense out of their own pockets. Private-company D&O usually comes packaged with EPLI for not much more money — going monoline EPLI gives up that protection.
findings.recommendation: At next renewal, market a Private Company Management Liability package (D&O + EPLI + Crime + Fiduciary) instead of monoline EPLI. Hartford, Travelers, Chubb, CNA all write packages for manufacturers. Typical premium increment for adding D&O to existing EPLI is modest. Verify entity coverage (Side C), Insured-vs.-Insured exclusion carve-backs, prior/pending litigation date.
discoveryQuestions: Who owns Precision Aero — single owner, family, partners, outside investors? How would those owners feel about being personally on the hook for a regulatory investigation defense?
If OSHA or the FAA opened a formal investigation tomorrow, who pays the lawyers — the company, or the executives personally?

If you ever sell the company or take outside investment, do you know that buyers/investors will require D&O tail coverage? It's much cheaper to set up the policy now than to start it at the deal table.
When you bought EPLI as a monoline policy instead of a Management Liability package, did anyone walk you through what you were giving up on the D&O and Crime side?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Crime / Fidelity Coverage
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No Crime / Fidelity / Social Engineering policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: No Crime policy in the disclosed program. Manufacturers face material employee-theft, forgery, computer-fraud, and social-engineering exposure: (a) bookkeeper/controller embezzlement (multi-year fraud schemes routinely exceed $250K), (b) fraudulent wire transfer requests via spoofed CEO/CFO email (six- and seven-figure losses are common), (c) check forgery, (d) inventory shrink. Without a Crime policy, every dollar lost is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: If your bookkeeper is skimming, your controller writes themselves checks, or someone spoofs an email from you and tricks the AP team into wiring $250K to a fake bank account — none of that is covered anywhere in your program right now. Crime policies are inexpensive and specifically built for these scenarios.
findings.recommendation: Bind Crime policy with $500K-$1M limits covering Employee Theft, Forgery & Alteration, Computer Fraud, Funds Transfer Fraud, and Social Engineering Fraud (the last must be specifically endorsed — not all forms include it). Verify Client Property coverage if Precision Aero handles customer-owned material. Include 'employee' definition broad enough to cover temps and leased workers.
discoveryQuestions: Who has check-writing authority and access to the company bank accounts at Precision Aero, and what's the dual-control process for outgoing wires?
Has anyone in AP ever received an urgent wire-transfer request that turned out to be from a spoofed email address?
When was the last time you ran a surprise audit on the books? Most embezzlement schemes run two to four years before they're caught.
If you discovered tomorrow that your controller had been moving $20K a month into a side account for three years, who reimburses the company — the bank, the policy, or nobody?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Products / Aerospace Products Liability
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No Products Liability or Aviation/Aerospace Products policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: Products/Completed Operations is normally part of CGL — but standard CGL policies frequently exclude or limit aerospace products (the 'aircraft products' exclusion). For a company named 'Precision Aero' working in aerospace, a standard CGL alone is typically inadequate; an Aviation Products Liability policy or an aerospace-friendly CGL with the aircraft-products exclusion deleted is required. Even if Precision Aero ultimately binds a CGL (Finding #015), it must be specifically vetted for aerospace products coverage. Without it, every part shipped that ends up in an aircraft is uninsured for downstream products liability.
findings.plain_english: Standard GL policies have a clause that says 'we don't cover anything that ends up on an aircraft.' If you're machining aerospace parts — and given your name, you probably are — a standard GL policy is essentially useless for your core product. You need either an aviation-products-specific policy or a GL with the aircraft exclusion specifically deleted, and the carrier has to be willing to underwrite it.
findings.recommendation: 1) Confirm Precision Aero's actual product mix — what percentage of revenue is for aerospace end-use? 2) When binding GL (Finding #015), require deletion of the Aircraft Products exclusion or bind a parallel Aviation Products Liability policy with a specialty carrier (Global Aerospace, Starr Aviation, AIG Aerospace). 3) Confirm flow-down indemnity language to suppliers and verify supplier insurance certificates.
discoveryQuestions: What percentage of what you machine ends up in an aircraft, helicopter, drone, or spacecraft?
Do your aerospace customers — Boeing, Lockheed, RTX, the Tier-1 suppliers — flow down product liability and indemnity requirements in their POs and master agreements?
If a part you machined was implicated in an aviation incident, who would be defending the case — you, your carrier, or the airframe OEM?
Has anyone walked through your current GL (if there is one) to confirm the aircraft-products exclusion is deleted, or are you assuming standard GL covers your aerospace work?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Pollution / Environmental Coverage
findings.contract_quote: No upstream contract requirement provided.
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No Pollution / Environmental Liability policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: Standard CGL policies (which Precision Aero does not currently appear to have) include a Total Pollution Exclusion. Manufacturing operations — particularly precision machining — generate cutting fluids, coolants, solvents, and metal swarf that constitute pollutants. Without a standalone Pollution Legal Liability or Premises Pollution policy, sudden-and-accidental and gradual releases are uninsured. Aerospace processes may also involve passivation chemicals, cleaners, and finishing operations with regulated effluents.
findings.plain_english: Even if you bind GL tomorrow, GL policies specifically exclude pollution. Cutting fluids, solvents, and finishing chemicals leaking into the floor drain, soil, or groundwater can rack up cleanup costs and regulatory fines fast. A Pollution policy is typically not expensive for a clean shop with good housekeeping.
findings.recommendation: Quote Premises Pollution Liability with $1M-$2M limits covering on-site cleanup, third-party bodily injury and property damage from pollution, transportation, and disposal-site coverage. Verify any used-oil, cutting-fluid, or chemical-disposal vendor agreements for indemnity flow-down.
discoveryQuestions: What chemicals, cutting fluids, and solvents do you use on the shop floor, and how are they stored and disposed of?
If a 55-gallon drum of cutting fluid leaked into the floor drain and reached the storm sewer, who would pay for the cleanup and the EPA fines?
Who picks up your used oil and cutting-fluid waste, and does their contract indemnify you if their truck spills on the way to the disposal site?
When was the last Phase I environmental on the building, and is there any history of prior tenant contamination on the parcel?

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions
findings.policy_quote: Disclosed program contains only USLI EPLI. No Professional Liability / E&O policy provided for audit.
findings.gap_description: Whether Professional Liability / E&O is needed depends on operations. Pure machining-to-print is a CGL/Products risk, not an E&O risk. But if Precision Aero performs ANY of the following, E&O is needed: (a) design or engineering services, (b) consulting on customer designs, (c) certification or testing services, (d) reverse-engineering, (e) sole-source design responsibility for any component. CGL covers bodily injury and property damage but does NOT cover economic loss from a design or specification error.
findings.plain_english: If you only machine what the customer's blueprint tells you to machine, you probably don't need this. But if you ever offer design suggestions, do reverse-engineering, or have any 'we know better than the print' responsibility on a part, GL won't cover an economic-loss claim from a design error — that's what E&O is for.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Precision Aero's scope of services: machine-to-print only, or any design/engineering/consulting/certification responsibility. If the latter, quote a Manufacturers' E&O or Miscellaneous Professional Liability policy with $1M-$2M limits.

findings.requirement_type: Program Gap — No Stop Gap (if any operations in monopolistic states)
findings.policy_quote: States of operation not specified in client notes. No Stop Gap endorsement evident.
findings.gap_description: If Precision Aero has any operations or employees in monopolistic WC states (North Dakota, Ohio, Washington, Wyoming), Employer's Liability coverage is NOT included in the state fund WC policy. A Stop Gap Employer's Liability endorsement on the GL policy is required to fill this gap. Cannot determine applicability without confirmed state list.
findings.plain_english: Four states sell their own Workers' Comp and don't include the lawsuit-defense piece — you have to buy that separately on your GL. If you have any people in North Dakota, Ohio, Washington, or Wyoming, this matters. If you don't, ignore it.
findings.recommendation: Confirm states of operation. If any monopolistic-state exposure, endorse Stop Gap Employer's Liability onto the (to-be-bound) GL policy.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Third-Party Harassment / Wrongful Acts Coverage
findings.policy_quote: Third-party coverage scope lives in EPL-J base form — text not available.
findings.gap_description: Third-party EPLI coverage responds to discrimination/harassment claims brought by NON-employees (customers, vendors, delivery drivers) alleging Precision Aero personnel harassed them. Manufacturers commonly face these from delivery drivers and contractor visits to the plant. Whether USLI EPL-J includes third-party coverage is not visible from the renewal certificate.
findings.plain_english: If a delivery driver claims one of your shift supervisors harassed them, that's not an employee-vs.-employer claim — it's a non-employee claim. Whether your EPLI covers that depends on a single line in the form we haven't seen yet.
findings.recommendation: Verify EPL-J third-party coverage scope. If absent or sublimited, request endorsement at next renewal — most EPLI carriers offer affirmative third-party coverage at no or minimal additional premium.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Punitive Damages Treatment
findings.policy_quote: Punitive damages treatment lives in EPL-J Loss definition + EPL-167 Amended Definition of Loss — text not available.
findings.gap_description: EPLI policies vary widely on punitive damages: (a) covered without restriction, (b) covered where insurable by law (most-favored-jurisdiction wording is best), (c) excluded entirely. For Arizona where this policy sits, punitive damages are insurable. EPL-167 'Amended Definition of Loss' specifically modifies what counts as covered Loss — could broaden or narrow punitive treatment, plus front pay, back pay, liquidated damages, and equitable relief.
findings.plain_english: Juries hand out punitive damages in employment cases all the time. Whether your policy pays them or leaves them with you depends on language we haven't seen. We need to read EPL-167 specifically.
findings.recommendation: Pull EPL-167 endorsement form text plus EPL-J Loss definition. Confirm punitive damages, front pay, back pay, and liquidated damages treatment. Most-favored-jurisdiction wording for punitives is best practice.

findings.requirement_type: Program-Wide — Single-Policy Program is Itself a Finding
findings.policy_quote: Only one policy disclosed in the program: USLI EPLI policy EPL1575392A.
findings.gap_description: If the disclosed program data is in fact complete, Precision Aero — an aerospace manufacturer — is operating with a single $1M EPLI policy and nothing else. This would mean no GL, no Auto, no WC, no Property, no Umbrella, no Cyber, no Crime, no D&O, no Products. Every category of meaningful business risk other than employment practices would be uninsured. This is functionally an uninsured business and constitutes the single largest finding of the audit. The more likely explanation is that additional policies exist but were not provided for analysis — but that itself is a critical audit-preparation issue.
findings.plain_english: If the documents you sent are everything you carry, this is the entire conversation. You have no GL, no auto, no WC, no property, no umbrella, no cyber — nothing but EPLI. Every other category of risk lands directly in your operating cash. The most urgent thing on this audit is not any specific gap — it's confirming whether the rest of the program exists somewhere else, and if it doesn't, getting it bound today.
findings.recommendation: STOP-WORK PRIORITY: Within 24 hours, confirm whether GL, Auto, WC, Property, Umbrella, Cyber, Crime, and D&O policies exist outside the documents provided. If they do, get them into the file and re-run the audit. If they don't, treat as a coverage emergency — bind a complete program (or interim binders) as the first action item, before continuing the detailed audit work.
discoveryQuestions: Help me make sure I'm not missing anything obvious — can you send me the declarations pages for your GL, Auto, WC, Property, Umbrella, and any other coverage you carry? Even just the Dec pages so I can confirm the program is what I think it is.

If everything you have is what's in the file, I need to ask directly: do you understand that you are operating an aerospace manufacturing business with employees, equipment, and product exposure, on a single EPLI policy and nothing else?
Who sold you the EPLI policy, and were they representing themselves as your full broker, or just placing the EPLI line?

Can we get on a call this week — not to talk about my recommendations, just to do a complete inventory of every policy you have, even ones you forgot about, so we know exactly where you stand before we move?

findings.requirement_type: Audit Scope Limitation — Contract Requirements Not Loaded
findings.contract_quote: N/A — no contract requirements were supplied to this analysis pass (requirements array empty).
findings.policy_quote: N/A
findings.gap_description: The contract requirements file passed into this audit was empty. Findings below are limited to the RMF checklist walk against the Pekin Workers' Compensation policy. Contract-vs-policy gap analysis (additional insured triggers, primary & noncontributory wording, indemnification flow-down, COI requirements, certificate-holder lists, designated entity NOC, etc.) has NOT been performed on this pass.
findings.plain_english: We audited the Workers' Comp policy on its own merits, but we have not yet been able to compare it against the contracts you have to live up to (customer MSAs, supplier agreements, lease agreements, etc.). The audit is therefore incomplete on the contract-compliance dimension. Once the upstream contract requirements are loaded, a second pass is needed.
findings.recommendation: Re-run the audit once Precision Aero's upstream contracts (Tier-1 supplier MSAs with OEMs/defense primes, lease agreements for the operating facility, any customer-imposed insurance schedules) have been extracted into the requirements set. Then verify the WC policy against each contractually-mandated insurance term.

When was the last time anyone read your customer contracts side-by-side with your insurance policies to confirm you actually meet the insurance requirements they impose?
Have you ever had a customer reject a Certificate of Insurance because something on it didn't match the contract — and if so, what was the issue?

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation Notice — 90-Day Broker Standard
findings.contract_quote: N/A — no contract requirements loaded; broker benchmark is 90 days.
findings.policy_quote: Standard WC policy cancellation provisions (WC 00 00 00 C) not contained in extracted excerpt — verify cancellation notice terms
findings.policy_page: Cancellation provisions not in the extracted dec / endorsement excerpt
findings.gap_description: The standard NCCI Workers' Compensation policy form (WC 00 00 00 C) cancellation provision was not included in the extracted excerpt. Standard WC cancellation is typically 10 days non-payment / 30 days for-cause. The Patriot benchmark is 90-day for-cause notice. There is also no Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement in the schedule, which would be needed if any customer / lessor / lender requires advance notice of cancellation.
findings.plain_english: We can't confirm from the documents we extracted what the cancellation notice period actually is on this policy, and we don't see a special endorsement that would notify your customers if the policy is cancelled. If a Tier-1 customer or your facility lease requires 30 or 60 days of advance notice of any cancellation, a standard policy may not satisfy that obligation.
findings.recommendation: Pull the full policy form to confirm cancellation notice periods for non-payment and for-cause. If any customer, lessor, or lender requires advance NOC, add a Designated Entity NOC endorsement and schedule them by name. Negotiate a 90-day for-cause notice if achievable in this market.
discoveryQuestions: If Pekin sent you a non-renewal notice tomorrow, who do you contractually have to notify before that date — your customers, your bank, your landlord — and how much warning are you required to give them?
Has a customer or lender ever asked to be listed as a 'notice party' on your insurance, and did you confirm the carrier actually issued an endorsement to back it up?

Walk me through what would happen operationally if your WC carrier non-renewed mid-contract on a Boeing or Lockheed program — would you be able to find replacement coverage fast enough to keep the contract intact?

findings.requirement_type: Unintentional Errors and Omissions Giveback
findings.contract_quote: N/A
findings.policy_quote: No Unintentional Errors and Omissions endorsement listed on the schedule of forms (Information Page, p. 1).
findings.policy_page: Page 1 — Information Page / schedule of forms
findings.gap_description: WC policies traditionally don't carry a separate Unintentional E&O endorsement (the WC form itself is statutory and the giveback concept is more common to GL). However, the broader RMF principle — that an inadvertent omission of a class code, payroll figure, or location should not void coverage — should be confirmed with Pekin. Verify the policy provides protection against good-faith reporting errors at audit.
findings.plain_english: If you accidentally underreport payroll or miss a class code at audit, will the carrier void the coverage on a claim, or will they just adjust the premium? The endorsement we'd typically look for to confirm the carrier won't penalize honest mistakes was not on the schedule. Combined with the Audit Noncompliance Charge that already lets Pekin charge up to 2x premium, this needs verification.
findings.recommendation: Ask Pekin in writing whether the policy contains an Unintentional E&O / inadvertent omission giveback (sometimes embedded in the carrier's WC form rather than a separate endorsement). Document the response.
discoveryQuestions: When you do payroll audit prep, who's actually responsible for making sure every job code and location is reported — and how confident are you that nothing slips through?
If your bookkeeper accidentally classified an aerospace machinist under a clerical code for six months, what's the worst outcome you've ever heard of from a carrier reacting to that kind of mistake?

findings.requirement_type: Named Insured — LLC Affiliate Reliably Added
findings.contract_quote: N/A
findings.policy_quote: WC 97 06 01 (01-20) — Amendment of Policy — Named Insured (Name Overflow): adds Black Mountain Investment Company LLC as Named Insured alongside Precision Aero Inc.
findings.policy_page: Page 3 of the WC PEKIN 24 policy
findings.gap_description: Precision Aero Inc (Corporation) is the primary Named Insured. Black Mountain Investment Company LLC — an affiliate likely holding real estate or investment assets — is added directly to the Named Insured field via WC 97 06 01 Name Overflow endorsement. Because this is a direct amendment to the Named Insured rather than a Broad Form Named Insured conditional extension, the LLC is reliably an insured employer under this WC policy. There is no GAP-01 LLC-exclusion concern on this policy.
findings.plain_english: Both your operating company (Precision Aero Inc) and your affiliate Black Mountain Investment Company LLC are properly named on the Workers' Comp policy. The way the LLC was added is the bulletproof way — it's written directly into the Named Insured field, not extended by a conditional endorsement that often quietly excludes LLCs. This is correct.
findings.recommendation: No action — keep this structure across renewals and confirm the same direct-amendment approach is used on every other line of coverage in the program (this is exactly what we'd want to see).

findings.requirement_type: Notice and Knowledge — Officer-Limited Trigger
findings.contract_quote: N/A
findings.policy_quote: No Notice and Knowledge / Imputation of Knowledge endorsement appears in the schedule of forms.
findings.policy_page: Information Page schedule of forms, page 1
findings.gap_description: There is no endorsement limiting 'notice of an occurrence' or 'knowledge of an occurrence' to the company's officers, the risk manager, or the person responsible for insurance. Under the unmodified WC policy, knowledge of any employee can be imputed to the entity. For a manufacturing operation with ~30+ employees on the floor, this means a shift lead's awareness of an incident that wasn't formally reported could later be used by the carrier to argue late-notice prejudice on a serious indemnity claim.
findings.plain_english: Right now, if any employee on the shop floor knew about an incident and didn't tell management, the carrier could argue you missed your reporting obligation — even if leadership genuinely didn't know. The fix is a one-page endorsement that says 'notice doesn't count until someone in leadership knows.' Cheap insurance, materially better protection.
findings.recommendation: Request a Notice & Knowledge / Imputation of Knowledge endorsement from Pekin that limits the trigger to the officer / risk manager / person responsible for insurance. If Pekin won't issue it on the WC, address the same point on the GL and Auto policies (where it's more commonly available).
discoveryQuestions: If a press operator told their shift lead about a near-miss but it never made it to your operations manager, would you expect that to count as 'the company knew' for insurance purposes?
How do incidents on the shop floor actually escalate from the employee level to the person responsible for insurance — and how confident are you that nothing falls through the cracks?
Have you ever had a claim where the carrier asked when you first knew about it, and you had to dig through emails to defend the timing?

findings.requirement_type: Waiver of Subrogation — Blanket WoS Endorsement
findings.contract_quote: N/A — contract requirements not loaded; however, Tier-1 aerospace/defense supplier contracts (Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop, RTX, primes serving DoD programs) virtually always require Waiver of Subrogation in favor of the customer on the Workers' Compensation policy.
findings.policy_quote: No Waiver of Subrogation endorsement (WC 00 03 13 — Waiver of Our Right to Recover from Others) appears in the schedule of endorsements on the Information Page.
findings.policy_page: Information Page schedule of forms, page 1
findings.gap_description: Pekin retains its full statutory right of subrogation against any third party whose negligence contributes to an employee injury. For an aerospace machine shop supplying OEMs and defense primes, this means: if a Precision Aero employee is injured on a customer's premises, or while working with a customer-supplied tool / fixture / drawing, Pekin's subrogated counsel can sue that customer to recover what it paid out. This directly violates the standard 'mutual waiver of subrogation' clause embedded in nearly every aerospace/defense Tier-1 supplier MSA. The carrier is not bound by Precision Aero's contract — only by what's endorsed on the policy.
findings.plain_english: Right now, if one of your guys gets hurt on a Boeing or Lockheed shop floor, your insurance carrier has the right to turn around and sue Boeing or Lockheed to recover what they paid. Your supplier agreements almost certainly forbid you from letting that happen — meaning if it does happen, you've personally breached the contract, and Boeing/Lockheed's lawyers come after Precision Aero (not the carrier) to make them whole. You'd be out-of-pocket for the same dollars the carrier already paid, plus legal fees, plus the relationship damage. A blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement closes this hole and is usually $250-$2,500/year.
findings.recommendation: Bind a blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement (WC 00 03 13 with 'Blanket — any person or organization with whom the insured has a written contract requiring waiver' wording) on this WC policy at the next available date — do not wait for renewal. Verify the cost. Also verify GL, Auto, and Umbrella each carry blanket WoS — this is a program-level concern, not just WC.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through the insurance section of your top supplier contract — does it require a Waiver of Subrogation in their favor on your Workers' Comp, and have you ever confirmed your carrier actually endorsed it?

If one of your machinists got hurt on a customer's premises tomorrow, who do you think would end up paying for that — and would you be surprised to learn your carrier could turn around and sue your customer?
Has your largest customer ever audited your COIs or pulled actual policy endorsements to verify the WoS language? What did they find?

If Pekin recovered $200k from Boeing on a subrogation action, and Boeing then sent you a breach-of-contract demand letter for that same $200k plus their legal fees, does Precision Aero have the cash on hand to absorb that — and does it cost you the program?

findings.requirement_type: All States Endorsement — Item 3.A vs 3.C Coverage Map
findings.contract_quote: N/A
findings.policy_quote: Part Three (Other States) covers all states and U.S. territories EXCEPT North Dakota, Ohio, Washington, Wyoming, Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands, and Arizona (which sits on Part One — Item 3.A).
findings.gap_description: Item 3.A (states where coverage is statutorily provided) lists Arizona. Item 3.C (Other States) sweeps in all remaining states and territories except the four monopolistic states (ND/OH/WA/WY) and the territories Pekin doesn't write in (PR/USVI). For a single-domicile AZ aerospace operation with potential field travel and customer-site visits, this is appropriately broad. There is no apparent state that was on 3.C last year and dropped this year (which would be a red flag).
findings.plain_english: If one of your team travels to do a quality audit, an installation, or a customer visit anywhere in the lower 48 outside the four monopolistic states, the policy picks them up automatically. That's the right structure for a manufacturer that occasionally puts boots on the ground at customer sites.
findings.recommendation: No action. At each renewal verify that no state listed last year has been dropped from 3.C — if a state moves off 3.C without anyone noticing, an injured employee in that state has zero coverage.

findings.requirement_type: Monopolistic State Exposure — ND / OH / WA / WY
findings.contract_quote: N/A
findings.policy_quote: Part Three excludes North Dakota, Ohio, Washington, and Wyoming.
findings.gap_description: The four monopolistic states (ND/OH/WA/WY) are statutorily required to be insured through their state-run funds — Pekin cannot provide WC coverage there. If Precision Aero has any employees travelling to, working at customer sites in, or temporarily relocated to any of these four states, separate state-fund WC coverage is required. Without it, an injury in any of those four states is fully uninsured.
findings.plain_english: There are four states — North Dakota, Ohio, Washington, and Wyoming — where the state runs the workers' comp system itself, and Pekin (or any private carrier) literally cannot cover you there. If you have anyone visiting customers, doing installations, or attending trade shows in those states, you need a separate state-fund policy — and right now we don't see one. We need to know if you have any exposure in those four states.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Precision Aero leadership: (a) whether any employees have travelled to or worked in ND, OH, WA, or WY in the past 12 months, and (b) whether any current or planned customer relationships will require travel there. If yes, set up coverage with the relevant state fund(s) AND add a Stop Gap (Employer's Liability) endorsement on the Pekin WC for the same states. If no, document that finding and re-confirm at renewal.
discoveryQuestions: In the past year, has anyone on your team — engineers, quality folks, sales, anyone — set foot in Ohio, Washington State, North Dakota, or Wyoming for work?
Do any of your customers have facilities in those four states where you might send someone for an installation, audit, or training?
If you sent a quality engineer to a customer site in Ohio next quarter, do you know whether your current WC policy would cover them if they got hurt?

findings.contract_quote: Broker benchmark RMF item — protects insured from coverage denial when an unreported location, vehicle, exposure, or operation later becomes the basis of a claim.

Neither Pekin policy carries this endorsement. With Precision Aero already operating under tight CGL guardrails (Designated Premises endorsement CG 21 60 limiting coverage to 5310 S 32nd St; Products entirely excluded), the absence of an Unintentional E&O giveback compounds the risk that a documentation slip — a new piece of equipment financed but not added to the schedule, a temporary off-site project, an acquired related entity — becomes a coverage-denial trigger.

The fix is a one-line endorsement called 'Unintentional Errors and Omissions' that says good-faith mistakes don't void coverage. It usually costs nothing.
findings.recommendation: Request Unintentional E&O giveback endorsements on both BOP and Umbrella. Verify the wording covers an unintentional failure to disclose, not just a misstatement.

findings.gap_description: Only the operating C-corp 'Precision Aero Inc' is named on either policy. There is no Broad Form Named Insured endorsement (e.g., ISO IL 00 17 or carrier proprietary BFNI form) extending automatic coverage to (a) related real-estate entities holding the 5310 S 32nd St property, (b) any holding company or affiliate, (c) retirement-plan trustee entities, or (d) JVs/teaming agreements common in aerospace supply work. The umbrella's reliance on Section II.2/II.7 is limited: II.2 covers only subsidiaries already covered by underlying at inception, and II.7 requires 90-day notice — both sit ABOVE missing scheduling on the underlying GL. If Precision Aero was sued together with a related entity, the related entity has no defense or indemnity.

If you own a separate real-estate LLC that holds the building, or an affiliate that handles purchasing, or a 401(k) trust — none of those entities have liability coverage. If a plaintiff sues your operating company AND your real-estate LLC together (which is what plaintiffs' attorneys do), the real-estate LLC has to defend itself. Adding a 'Broad Form Named Insured' endorsement gives automatic coverage to all entities you own or control.

(2) Confirm Pekin's BFNI wording does NOT exclude LLCs or partnerships from automatic extension (some BFNI forms only auto-cover corporations). findings.requirement_type: Notice & Knowledge of Occurrence (cross-program)
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — the carrier should only require notice of an occurrence when an officer, the person responsible for insurance, or the risk manager has actual knowledge.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CG 00 01 10 01 — base CGL 'Duties In The Event Of Occurrence, Offense, Claim Or Suit' applies without endorsement carve-back limiting knowledge to designated officers. Umbrella Section IV.6 (CU 00 01 08 22, Pg 11ish): 'You must see to it that we, or any underlying insurer, are notified as soon as practicable of an occurrence ...' — no carve-back limiting knowledge to person responsible for insurance.
findings.gap_description: Neither policy is endorsed with a 'Notice & Knowledge' (sometimes 'Knowledge of Occurrence,' 'Imputation of Knowledge,' or 'Notice Manager') giveback. As written, ANY employee's knowledge of an occurrence can be imputed to Precision Aero, starting the notice clock. In a 75-employee machine shop, a shop-floor lead's failure to escalate a tool-strike incident to management can later be argued by the carrier as untimely notice — voiding coverage. The umbrella replicates the same broad notice obligation. The umbrella is excluded from a self-standing notice endorsement only because it should follow form to the underlying CGL — but the CGL itself doesn't have one, so neither layer protects the insured.
findings.plain_english: Today, if a machinist on second shift sees a near-miss or a part failure and doesn't tell management, the law treats Precision Aero as having known about it the moment the machinist did. If a claim shows up six months later and the carrier learns the shop-floor employee knew first, they can deny based on late notice. Adding a 'Notice & Knowledge' endorsement says: only when a named officer or the person responsible for insurance has actual knowledge does the notice clock start. This is a no-brainer endorsement.
findings.recommendation: Request Notice & Knowledge endorsement on the underlying BOP CGL (and on the Pekin Auto and EL policies not in this audit batch). Verify it limits imputed knowledge to named officers / risk-management point-of-contact. Once endorsed on each underlying line, the umbrella conditional follow-form will pick it up.
discoveryQuestions: If a CNC operator on second shift saw a tool break and a piece fly toward another worker but no one was hurt — would they tell their supervisor, would the supervisor escalate, and how long until your insurance point-of-contact would actually hear about it?
Have you ever had a claim where a carrier questioned how quickly the incident was reported up your chain of command? What was the outcome?
Who in your organization — by name and title — is the official point-of-contact for insurance reporting? Does every supervisor know to route incidents to that person?

findings.requirement_type: Waiver of Subrogation — Blanket (cross-program)
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — blanket Waiver of Subrogation by written contract on GL, Auto, Property, and WC, BEST PRACTICES wording.
findings.policy_quote: BOP checklist field 'waiver_of_subrogation': false; no CG 24 04 (Blanket Waiver) on the endorsement schedule. Umbrella Section IV.8 — standard Transfer of Rights of Recovery; no Waiver-of-Subrogation giveback. Umbrella checklist 'waiver_of_subrogation': false.
findings.policy_page: BOP endorsement schedule; Umbrella Section IV.8
findings.gap_description: No Blanket Waiver of Subrogation (CG 24 04 or equivalent) is endorsed on the BOP CGL or Property. The Umbrella has no follow-form waiver giveback in Section IV.8. Aerospace customer purchase orders and supplier MSAs commonly require a waiver of subrogation in favor of the customer (Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop, Honeywell, Raytheon, and tier-1 primes routinely require this). Without a blanket waiver, every customer agreement that contains a subrogation-waiver requirement creates a contractual breach risk AND, if Pekin later subrogates against a customer after a claim, can damage the customer relationship and trigger Precision Aero's hold-harmless to the customer.
findings.plain_english: When you sign a contract with Boeing, Lockheed, or any major aerospace prime, the contract usually says 'your insurance company can't sue us to recover money even if we caused the loss.' Right now your policy doesn't agree to that. So either (a) you're technically in breach of every customer contract that requires it, or (b) Pekin pays a claim and then sues your customer to recover, which destroys the customer relationship. The fix is a 'blanket waiver of subrogation' endorsement that automatically waives Pekin's recovery rights any time you sign a contract requiring it.
findings.recommendation: Request CG 24 04 11 85 (Waiver of Transfer of Rights of Recovery Against Others — Blanket) on the BOP CGL, blanket Waiver of Subrogation on the Auto and WC policies (not in this audit batch), CP 12 99 or carrier equivalent on Property, and a follow-form blanket waiver giveback on the Umbrella. Verify all use 'where required by written contract executed prior to loss' language.
discoveryQuestions: Pull up your supplier agreement with your largest aerospace customer — does it include a 'waiver of subrogation' clause requiring your insurer to give up its recovery rights against them?
If Pekin paid a $500,000 claim tomorrow and then sued one of your top-3 customers to recover the money, what would that do to your relationship and your purchase orders?
Have any of your customers refused to issue a PO until they got a certificate showing waiver of subrogation in their favor? How was that resolved last time?

findings.requirement_type: Additional Insured — Blanket vs Scheduled
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — blanket AI 'where required by written contract' is the standard for any commercial operation that signs customer or vendor agreements.
findings.policy_quote: BOP additional_insureds list contains only scheduled entities: Makino Inc, Black Mountain Aerospace (CG 20 28 07 04 — equipment lessor); Wells Fargo Equipment Finance, Zions Bancorporation/National Bank of AZ (481TPR manuscript). BOP checklist 'additional_insured_blanket': false; 'additional_insured_completed_ops': false. No CG 20 33 (Blanket AI — Ongoing Ops) or CG 20 37 (Blanket AI — Completed Ops) attached.
findings.gap_description: BOP only provides AI status to specifically scheduled entities — and the AI grants are narrow: CG 20 28 covers only liability arising from leased equipment, ongoing ops only, terminating with the lease. There is no blanket AI 'where required by written contract' endorsement. Every aerospace customer that requires AI status under their PO or MSA either (a) does not have it, putting Precision Aero in contractual breach and exposing them to indemnification obligations the policy won't reach, or (b) has to be specifically endorsed at additional broker effort. Combined with Products-Completed Operations being entirely excluded (separate finding), AI for Completed Ops is impossible on this policy as written.
findings.plain_english: Most of your aerospace customers' purchase orders require you to add them as an 'additional insured' on your insurance. Right now your policy only does that for two equipment vendors and your two equipment finance lenders — nobody else. Every customer relationship that needs AI status creates either (a) a contract breach, or (b) a one-off endorsement request. The fix is a 'blanket additional insured' endorsement that automatically grants AI status to any party you've signed a contract requiring it — for ongoing ops AND completed operations.
findings.recommendation: Request CG 20 33 (Blanket AI — Ongoing Ops, automatic status) AND CG 20 37 (Blanket AI — Completed Ops). Note: the Completed Ops AI is moot until the products-completed operations exclusion (separate finding) is removed. Address both together as a package fix.
discoveryQuestions: Pull a representative aerospace customer PO — does it require you to add them as an 'additional insured on a primary and non-contributory basis'? How many active customer contracts have similar language right now?
When a customer asks for an additional insured certificate today, what's the process — does our office have to request a one-off endorsement from Pekin every time?
If a Boeing tier-1 prime audited your insurance compliance and found you only had two scheduled AIs, what would the consequence be on your supplier rating?

findings.requirement_type: Care, Custody and Control — Customer Property
findings.contract_quote: Aerospace machine shops routinely receive customer-supplied tooling, fixtures, raw forgings, work-in-process, and finished customer parts to be machined or assembled.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 10 01 Section I.2.j(4): excludes property damage to '[p]ersonal property in the care, custody or control of the insured.'
