No bailee endorsement, no Property Of Others Inland Marine sublimit beyond the BOP Property Personal Property of Others limit ($1,500,000 — Property only, not liability) is in the program.
findings.policy_page: BOP Pg 6 (base CGL); Property limits Pg 6
findings.gap_description: Aerospace machining is a CCC-heavy operation: customers ship in raw billets, forgings, semi-finished assemblies, expensive tooling and fixtures (often customer-furnished equipment, or 'CFE'), and Precision Aero performs work on them in their custody. The BOP CGL flatly excludes property damage to property in CCC. The BOP Property side has Personal Property of Others $1.5M — but that's first-party property coverage on Precision Aero's premises, NOT third-party liability coverage for damage to a customer's property in transit, at a sub-tier vendor, or after acceptance. A $200K titanium forging dropped during a setup, a customer fixture damaged in fixturing, a tier-1's CFE galled during machining — all uninsured for liability. The risk is squarely an aerospace exposure where customer parts can be worth $50K–$500K each.
findings.plain_english: Your customers ship you their parts and tooling — sometimes worth six figures each — for you to machine. The minute that property is in your shop, your CGL refuses to pay for damage to it, because the policy excludes 'property in your care, custody, or control.' Your Property policy has a $1.5M 'Personal Property of Others' limit, but that only covers things on your premises; it doesn't help if you damage a customer's part in transit, or at a subcontractor. A single ruined titanium forging or a damaged customer fixture could leave Precision Aero on the hook personally. The fix is a 'Bailee' or 'Property of Others' liability endorsement, OR a standalone Inland Marine policy specifically covering customer property.
findings.recommendation: (1) Quantify maximum value of customer property on premises and in transit at any one time. (2) Place a standalone Bailee / Inland Marine Property Of Others Liability policy (or endorsement) with limit matching the maximum exposure plus a buffer. (3) Confirm coverage extends to (a) customer property in transit, (b) at sub-tier suppliers, (c) post-shipment but before customer acceptance. (4) Coordinate with the BOP Personal Property of Others $1.5M to avoid double-coverage gaps and overlap.
discoveryQuestions: What's the highest-value single customer part or piece of customer-furnished tooling you've had on the shop floor in the last 12 months — and what was its replacement value?
If a $250,000 titanium forging dropped during a fixture setup tomorrow, who pays — and what does that customer relationship look like 30 days later?
Do any of your customer POs include a 'risk of loss passes on acceptance' clause — meaning you bear the risk while it's in your shop?
Do you ever ship customer parts to a sub-tier vendor for heat treat, plating, or NDI? Who's insuring the part while it's in transit?

findings.requirement_type: Contractual Liability — Insured Contract Definition
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — the CGL must support the insured's contractual indemnity obligations through the standard 'insured contract' definition without endorsements that narrow it.
findings.policy_quote: BOP forms list (Pg 6) includes CG 21 39 10 93 — Contractual Liability Limitation. This endorsement strikes the broad 'insured contract' definition in CG 00 01 paragraph 9.f and replaces it with a narrowed list of enumerated contract types.
findings.policy_page: BOP Pg 6 (forms schedule); CG 21 39 10 93 form text
findings.gap_description: CG 21 39 strikes paragraph (f) of the standard 'insured contract' definition — the catch-all 'that part of any other contract or agreement pertaining to your business ... under which you assume the tort liability of another party.' What remains is a narrow list (lease of premises, sidetrack, easement, indemnity to municipality, elevator maintenance, railroad). Almost every commercial customer PO, supplier MSA, distribution agreement, and tooling-loan agreement Precision Aero signs falls under (f) — and (f) is GONE. So the contractual indemnities Precision Aero accepts in customer agreements (the broad 'we'll defend and indemnify Boeing for any claim arising out of our work') get NO contractual liability coverage. A customer claim under that indemnity hits Precision Aero personally, with the CGL refusing to defend or pay because contractual liability coverage was endorsed away.
findings.plain_english: Every aerospace customer makes you sign a contract that says 'Precision Aero defends and pays Boeing/Lockheed/etc. if anything goes wrong with the work you did for us.' That promise is called 'contractual liability,' and your CGL is supposed to back it up. Pekin attached an endorsement (CG 21 39) that strips out the standard contractual liability coverage — leaving only a narrow list of leases, sidetrack agreements, and elevator-maintenance contracts. Customer indemnities are NOT on that list. So if Boeing demands you pay them under the indemnity in your supplier agreement, your CGL refuses. This is a major structural defect.
findings.recommendation: (1) Demand removal of CG 21 39 10 93 at next renewal — restoring the standard 'insured contract' definition under CG 00 01 9.f. (2) If carrier refuses, treat this as a placement defect and shop the program to a market that does not narrow contractual liability. (3) Until removed, audit every customer PO/MSA for the indemnity language and quantify the largest exposure that depends on contractual liability coverage.
discoveryQuestions: Pull your supplier agreement with your largest aerospace customer — what indemnification language do you owe them, and have you ever quantified your potential exposure under that clause?
If a Boeing or Lockheed prime invoked the indemnity clause in your supplier agreement after a claim — has anyone explained to you that your current CGL has been amended to NOT back that promise up?
When was the last time someone reviewed your customer contracts side-by-side against your CGL contractual-liability endorsement to confirm coverage flows through?

findings.requirement_type: Contractual Liability for Personal & Advertising Injury
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — the CGL Coverage B contractual liability exclusion should be endorsed back via CG 22 74 or carrier equivalent for indemnities involving advertising or personal injury.
findings.policy_quote: Base CG 00 01 10 01 Coverage B Section I.2.e excludes Personal & Advertising Injury 'for which the insured has assumed liability in a contract or agreement.' No endorsement restoring contractual liability for P&AI is in the BOP forms list.
findings.gap_description: Coverage B contractual liability is excluded under base CG 00 01 with no carve-back endorsed. Less material than the Coverage A Contractual Liability Limitation, but still notable when supplier or distribution agreements include advertising co-op or co-branding indemnities, trademark/use indemnities, or media-related hold-harmless clauses.
findings.plain_english: If you co-brand a product with a customer, run a joint marketing piece, or sign an indemnity around how a customer's logo is used on your website or trade-show booth, your policy won't back up that contractual indemnity for advertising/personal-injury claims. Lower-probability for an aerospace machine shop, but worth flagging.
findings.recommendation: Request CG 22 74 (Limited Contractual Liability — Personal And Advertising Injury) or carrier equivalent if any contracts include media, advertising, trademark, or co-branding indemnities.
discoveryQuestions: Do any of your customer or distributor agreements include co-branding, joint advertising, or trademark/logo-use indemnification language?
Have you ever been asked to indemnify a customer for marketing or advertising use of your name, logo, or capabilities?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — Absolute Exclusion + No Standalone Cyber
findings.contract_quote: Aerospace primes (Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop, Raytheon) routinely require CMMC / NIST 800-171 compliance and cyber insurance with breach-response coverage in supplier agreements.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CG 29 26 03 22 (Pg 22) — Exclusion: Access or Disclosure of Confidential or Personal Information and Data-Related Liability. Excludes 'damages arising out of: (1) Any access to or disclosure of any person's or organization's confidential or personal information ... (2) the loss of, loss of use of, damage to, corruption of, inability to access, or inability to manipulate electronic data.' Umbrella CU 00 56 06 22 (Pg 20) — same exclusion at umbrella WITHOUT the limited bodily-injury exception. Inland Marine CM 75 03 02 21 (Pg 27) — Cyber Incident Exclusion on the Motor Transit Cargo coverage. No standalone Cyber policy in this program.
findings.policy_page: BOP Pg 22 (CG 29 26); Umbrella Pg 20 (CU 00 56); BOP Pg 27 (CM 75 03)
findings.gap_description: All three coverage parts (BOP CGL, Umbrella, IM Motor Transit) carry absolute cyber exclusions. The umbrella version (CU 00 56) is the harshest variant — excludes BI, PD, Personal Injury, AND Advertising Injury arising from any data breach or electronic data event, with no bodily-injury carve-back. There is no standalone Cyber Liability policy in the program. Aerospace contractors are explicit cyber targets: ITAR/EAR-controlled data, controlled unclassified information (CUI), supplier-portal credentials, NIST 800-171 / CMMC compliance obligations, ransomware against MES/ERP/CNC controllers (a real threat — Norsk Hydro, ASCO, Boeing's 2018 WannaCry incident). A ransomware event hitting Precision Aero's CNC controllers, business email compromise stealing wire-transfer funds, or a CUI breach triggering DFARS 7012 notification all have ZERO coverage anywhere in this program.
findings.plain_english: Every part of your insurance program — your CGL, your umbrella, even the cargo policy on your delivery truck — has a hard exclusion for anything cyber-related: data breaches, ransomware, business email compromise, hacked CNC machines, stolen customer drawings. There is NO cyber policy anywhere in your program. For an aerospace shop with ITAR-controlled drawings and CMMC compliance obligations, this is one of the largest uninsured exposures on the program. A single ransomware event at a comparable shop typically runs $250K–$2M in restoration, ransom, business-interruption, and regulatory costs.
findings.recommendation: (1) Place a standalone Cyber Liability policy. Minimum coverages: first-party (ransomware/extortion sublimit at full policy limit, business interruption with manufacturing/dependent BI extension, system restoration), third-party (privacy and network security liability, regulatory defense including DFARS 7012/CMMC), social engineering / fraudulent funds transfer ($250K minimum), media liability. (2) Confirm coverage for ITAR-controlled data and DoD CUI. (3) Limit benchmark for an aerospace machine shop: $2M–$5M minimum. (4) Coordinate the cyber retroactive date as far back as commercially obtainable.
discoveryQuestions: Are any of your customer drawings, specifications, or supplier-portal credentials ITAR or DFARS-controlled? If those got into the wrong hands, what's the regulatory and customer fallout?

Walk me through what would happen if your CNC controllers and ERP system got encrypted by ransomware tonight — how long before you ship the next part, and what does your cash burn look like during that downtime?
Have any of your aerospace customers asked for evidence of cyber insurance or CMMC Level 2 certification in the last 12 months? What were they asking for in dollar terms?
Do you wire-transfer payments to vendors based on emailed wire instructions? If a fraudster impersonated a vendor and you sent $150K to the wrong account, who pays?

findings.requirement_type: Damage to Premises Rented to You — Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — the Damage to Premises Rented limit must be sized against the likely fire/legal-liability exposure for the rented premises.
findings.policy_quote: BOP Dec — 'Damage To Premises Rented To You' = $100,000 each occurrence.
findings.gap_description: Damage to Premises Rented to You = $100K. Standard CGL default is $100K but this is materially low for an industrial machine shop in Phoenix. The BOP separately schedules $1,081,600 of 'Property Legal Liability' on the Property side, suggesting Pekin is layering Tenants Legal Liability on the Property side rather than expanding the CGL sublimit. Worth confirming the Property Legal Liability $1.08M (a) actually responds to fire/water/explosion damage to the building Precision Aero rents, (b) is NOT subject to standard CGL exclusions, and (c) does not limit perils to fire only. If the $100K CGL is the only response to a non-fire peril, the gap is real.
findings.plain_english: The CGL only covers $100,000 if you damage the building you rent. That's typical for office space but low for a machine shop where a CNC fire, hydraulic blowout, or coolant-system failure could cause six- or seven-figure damage to the building. There's $1.08M of 'Property Legal Liability' on the Property side that may fill the gap — but it needs to be confirmed in writing that it responds to perils beyond fire. We should request the CGL Damage to Premises sublimit be increased to match the Property Legal Liability layer.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm in writing with Pekin whether 'Property Legal Liability' $1,081,600 covers all-perils tenants legal liability or fire-only. (2) If fire-only, increase Damage to Premises Rented sublimit to $1M+ on CGL via CG 23 79 (Damage to Premises Rented — Increased Limit) or carrier equivalent. (3) Verify limit matches landlord's lease requirement.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: BOP Property Legal Liability $1,081,600 — confirm peril scope
discoveryQuestions: Pull your lease for 5310 S 32nd St — what does the landlord require for tenants legal liability or fire legal liability?

If a CNC fire spread to the building structure tonight and caused $750,000 of damage, do you know whether Pekin's CGL or Property side responds — and would the $100K CGL sublimit be the binding limit?

findings.requirement_type: Duty to Defend
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — duty-to-defend is preferred for CGL.
findings.policy_quote: Base CG 00 01 10 01 Section I.1.a — 'We will have the right and duty to defend the insured against any "suit" seeking those damages.'
findings.gap_description: Standard CGL duty to defend is in place. Pekin retains the right to select counsel — which is the standard tradeoff. Worth confirming the insured understands the carrier picks counsel.
findings.plain_english: Pekin has a legal duty to defend you against covered lawsuits. They pick the lawyer, and they pay defense costs in addition to your policy limit. This is the standard, expected setup — it is correct.
findings.recommendation: No change. Confirm with insured they understand carrier-selected counsel applies; if they want choice of counsel for sensitive litigation, that requires a separate negotiation.

findings.requirement_type: Employee Benefits Liability — Retroactive Date
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — claims-made EBL coverage retroactive date should reach back to the inception of the insured's benefits administration to avoid prior-acts gaps.
findings.policy_quote: EB 00 02 07 97 (Pg 11): EBL Each Claim $1,000,000 / Aggregate $3,000,000; Retroactive Date 03/01/2016; $1,000 deductible each claim.
findings.gap_description: EBL is claims-made with a 03/01/2016 retroactive date — meaning negligent acts/errors/omissions in benefits administration committed before 03/01/2016 are uninsured even if the claim is made today. Precision Aero has presumably administered benefits for longer than 8 years; any error from those earlier years (incorrect 401(k) eligibility, misenrollment, COBRA notification failure, dependent-coverage misadministration) that surfaces as a claim post-3/1/2016 has no coverage. Confirm whether prior EBL existed before 03/01/2016 — if so, the retroactive date should be pulled back; if not, the 8-year exposed tail is what it is.
findings.plain_english: Your benefits administration coverage only protects against mistakes made AFTER March 1, 2016. If a former employee discovers in 2026 that someone in HR made a 401(k) eligibility mistake in 2014, that claim is uninsured. We need to confirm whether you had this coverage before 2016 — if yes, we should ask Pekin to push the retroactive date back to that earlier inception.
findings.recommendation: (1) Determine whether Precision Aero had EBL or fiduciary-related coverage before 03/01/2016. (2) If yes, request retroactive date be pulled back to original inception. (3) If no, document the prior-acts gap for client awareness and confirm $1M each claim / $3M aggregate is adequate against the benefits-administration error exposure.
discoveryQuestions: When did Precision Aero start providing employee benefits — health, 401(k), life — to its employees? Was that before or after March 2016?
Did you have any kind of fiduciary or employee-benefits-administration insurance before March 2016, and do we have copies of those policies?
Has anyone — employee or former employee — ever questioned whether their benefits eligibility, contribution, or COBRA notice was handled correctly?

findings.requirement_type: Employment Practices Liability — Excluded + No Standalone EPLI
findings.contract_quote: EEOC charges, harassment claims, wrongful termination claims, and wage-and-hour class actions are all everyday employer exposures.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CG 21 47 07 98 — Employment-Related Practices Exclusion. Excludes BI/PD/PI&AI 'arising out of any... refusal to employ ... termination of that person's employment ... [or] employment-related practices, policies, acts or omissions.' Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.f — Discrimination Exclusion: 'any alleged or actual discrimination by an insured against any person.' No standalone EPLI policy in this program.
findings.policy_page: BOP Pg 6 (CG 21 47); Umbrella Pg 9 Section I.2.f
findings.gap_description: CGL excludes employment practices via CG 21 47, and the umbrella has its own discrimination exclusion. There is no standalone EPLI policy in the program. Common employer claims — harassment, hostile work environment, wrongful termination, retaliation, wage-and-hour, FMLA/ADA disputes, EEOC charges — have ZERO coverage anywhere in the program. For a 75-employee Phoenix manufacturer in an industrial workforce, the exposure is concrete: EEOC charges run $50K–$250K to defend through resolution; class-action wage-and-hour can hit $1M+; California/AZ-specific Pregnancy and FEHA-equivalent claims are common.
findings.plain_english: If a former employee files an EEOC charge for harassment or wrongful termination, you have zero insurance coverage anywhere on this program. The CGL has an explicit employment-practices exclusion; the umbrella has a separate discrimination exclusion; nothing else in your program responds. Defending a single EEOC charge through resolution typically runs $75K–$200K out of pocket — and class wage-and-hour claims can run seven figures. EPLI coverage is widely available, usually $5K–$15K per million in limit for a manufacturer this size.
findings.recommendation: Place a standalone EPLI policy. Minimum recommended: $1M each claim / $1M aggregate, third-party coverage included (harassment/discrimination by non-employees), wage-and-hour defense-only sublimit (typically $100K–$250K), prior-and-pending date as far back as obtainable. Match limit to umbrella attachment if EPLI is intended to feed the umbrella (most umbrellas exclude EPL — confirm).
discoveryQuestions: How many employees do you have today, and what's been your turnover in the last 24 months?
Have you had any EEOC charges, harassment complaints, or wrongful-termination disputes in the last 5 years — even if they didn't go anywhere?
Do you have an HR department and a written employee handbook? When was the last time it was reviewed by employment counsel?
Are any of your supervisors handling discipline or termination decisions without HR review? If a fired employee sued for wrongful termination tomorrow, who'd defend you and pay the legal bills?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / Manufacturers E&O — Excluded + Missing
findings.contract_quote: Aerospace machine shops that perform any design, drafting, specification, or engineered-component work face professional-services exposure not covered by CGL.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CG 21 75 01 15 (Engineers, Architects or Surveyors Professional Liability) AND CG 21 76 01 15 (Designated Professional Services). Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.g — Professional Liability Exclusion: 'damages because of "professional liability,"' as broadly defined in Section V.15 (engineers, architects, surveyors, draftsmen explicitly listed). No standalone E&O / Manufacturers E&O / Professional Liability policy in this program.
findings.policy_page: BOP Pg 6 (CG 21 75/76); Umbrella Pg 9 Section I.2.g
findings.gap_description: CGL has both CG 21 75 (engineers/architects/surveyors PL) AND CG 21 76 (Designated Professional Services) — wholesale stripping of professional services exposure. Umbrella mirrors with its own broad PL exclusion. There is no standalone Professional Liability or Manufacturers E&O policy in the program. For an aerospace machine shop, the exposure depends on whether Precision Aero performs ANY of: design assistance, design-for-manufacturability input, first-article inspection sign-off, process specification, engineered-components-to-print, or any work where 'fitness for purpose' or 'as designed' could be the question (vs. simply 'made to customer print'). If they do any design work, this is a critical uninsured gap. Even if they're build-to-print only, customer claims often allege 'should have known the design was wrong' — defense costs alone can be devastating.
findings.plain_english: Your CGL only covers bodily injury and property damage — it does NOT cover claims that say 'your part didn't work as designed' or 'your inspection process missed a defect.' Pekin attached two endorsements to make sure professional-services claims are excluded, and the umbrella has the same exclusion. There is no E&O / Professional Liability policy in your program. If a customer says a part you made underperformed, didn't meet spec, or failed inspection — you have no defense or indemnity. For an aerospace shop where a single defective part can cause an in-flight or ground incident, this is one of the largest gaps on the program. A Manufacturers E&O policy is the standard fix.
findings.recommendation: (1) Place a Manufacturers E&O / Products E&O policy. (2) Minimum limit benchmark for aerospace component manufacturer: $2M–$5M each claim / $5M aggregate. (3) Confirm definition of 'professional services' includes design assistance, DFM, first-article sign-off, inspection certification, and any engineering input — not just stamped-engineer work. (4) Coordinate retroactive date to inception of operations, or as far back as obtainable. (5) Coordinate with Products Liability solution (separate finding) — many aerospace E&O markets bundle Products + E&O.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through what 'professional services' means in your operation — do you ever provide design input, DFM feedback, process recommendations, or engineering certifications back to your customers?
Do any of your engineers stamp drawings, sign first-article inspection reports, or certify processes? If yes, what's that signature exposure if a part later fails?
If a Boeing tier-1 prime claimed your part didn't meet spec — not that it caused injury, just that it underperformed — who would defend you, and where in your insurance program is that covered?
How many parts do you ship in a typical year, and what's your warranty/return process when a customer claims a defect?

findings.requirement_type: Fellow Employee Coverage — CGL
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF CGL-20 — Fellow Employee Exclusion should be deleted via CG 24 31 or carrier equivalent so that one employee suing another (in their official capacity) has insured defense.
findings.policy_quote: Base CG 00 01 10 01 Section II.2.a(1)(a) — 'employee' is not insured for BI to '[a] co-"employee" while in the course of his or her employment.' No CG 24 31 (Deletion of Fellow Employee Exclusion) endorsement on the schedule.
findings.gap_description: Standard CGL excludes liability of one employee to another. WC is the primary response for employee-vs-employee BI in the workplace, but where (a) the suing employee opts out of WC exclusivity (rare but possible — intentional-act allegations, gross-negligence carve-outs in some states), (b) family of an injured employee sues a supervisor or a co-employee personally, or (c) an off-the-clock altercation between employees occurs, the supervisor/co-employee has no CGL defense or indemnity. CG 24 31 deletes the exclusion and gives the co-employee defendant a defense.
findings.plain_english: If two of your employees got into a workplace dispute — say a supervisor disciplined a worker who later sued the supervisor personally — your CGL won't pay for the supervisor's defense or any judgment. WC handles the worker's medical and lost wages, but it doesn't defend the supervisor against being sued personally. Adding 'CG 24 31' deletes that exclusion and gives the supervisor (and any co-employee) a defense.
findings.recommendation: Request CG 24 31 (Deletion of Fellow Employee Exclusion) on the BOP CGL. Coordinate with WC policy review — many states' WC exclusivity protects most fellow-employee suits, but the carve-back closes the gap for the unusual cases.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: WC handles the injured employee's claim; this gap is for defense of the SUED co-employee/supervisor, which WC does NOT cover.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever had two employees get into a workplace altercation that escalated to a lawsuit — even one that was settled quietly?
If a supervisor disciplined a worker on the floor and that worker filed a personal lawsuit naming the supervisor by name, who pays the supervisor's lawyer?

findings.requirement_type: Hired & Non-Owned Auto — Coverage Confirmation
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — HNOA must be in place wherever employees use personal vehicles for company business or rented vehicles are used.
findings.policy_quote: BOP only carries Inland Marine Motor Transit Cargo on a 2018 Dodge Ram 1500 ($320K cargo limit). The Umbrella Schedule of Underlying lists 'Pekin Auto $1M CSL' — a separate Pekin commercial auto policy that was NOT provided in this audit batch.
findings.policy_page: BOP Pg 10 (Motor Transit Cargo); Umbrella Schedule of Underlying
findings.gap_description: A Pekin Commercial Auto policy at $1M CSL is referenced as underlying to the umbrella but was not provided in this audit batch. Without seeing the auto policy, HNOA confirmation cannot be made. HNOA is critical for Precision Aero — employees driving personal vehicles to customer sites for sales meetings, deliveries, banking runs, or AOG (aircraft-on-ground) emergency runs all create non-owned auto liability that the operating CGL does not cover.
findings.plain_english: There's a separate auto insurance policy referenced on your umbrella but it wasn't included in this audit. We need to pull and review the actual Auto policy to confirm Hired & Non-Owned Auto is on it — that's the coverage that responds when an employee uses their personal car for company business. Without HNOA, an employee's personal-auto crash on a sales call could leave Precision Aero personally exposed.
findings.recommendation: Request the Pekin Commercial Auto policy (referenced as underlying $1M CSL) and complete the Auto RMF walk in a follow-up audit pass.

findings.requirement_type: Mental Anguish in Bodily Injury Definition — CGL
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF CGL-23 — Mental Anguish standalone (not tied to physical bodily injury) should be in the BI definition.
findings.policy_quote: Base CG 00 01 10 01 Section V.3 — '"Bodily injury" means bodily injury, sickness or disease sustained by a person, including death resulting from any of these at any time.' Standard ISO definition does not include mental anguish standalone. No endorsement broadening the BI definition is on the BOP forms list.
findings.gap_description: Mental anguish, emotional distress, and shock are NOT included in the standard ISO BI definition unless tied to a physical injury. Many courts have held that emotional-distress damages (witnessing a coworker injury, witnessing a vehicle accident, post-traumatic stress from a workplace event) require BI to encompass mental anguish to be covered. RMF best practice is to endorse BI to include mental anguish standalone.
findings.plain_english: The CGL's definition of 'bodily injury' is the old narrow one — it covers physical injury and death but does NOT cover pure emotional or mental injury that doesn't involve a physical wound. If a witness to a workplace incident sues for PTSD or emotional distress without a physical injury, the policy may not respond. The fix is a one-line endorsement broadening 'bodily injury' to include mental anguish.
findings.recommendation: Request endorsement amending CG 00 01 V.3 to include mental anguish, emotional distress, mental injury, and shock — standalone, not requiring physical injury. Carrier-specific form numbers vary; ask Pekin for their amendment-of-BI-definition giveback.
discoveryQuestions: If a worker witnessed a coworker's serious shop-floor injury and later sued for PTSD without being physically hurt themselves, do you know if your CGL would respond to that suit?
Have you had any workplace incidents where a non-injured witness raised psychological-injury concerns?

findings.requirement_type: Per Project / Per Location Aggregate — CGL
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF — for an insured operating across multiple projects or locations, a Per Project (CG 25 03) or Per Location (CG 25 04) aggregate prevents one project's loss from eroding aggregate available for another.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CGL Dec — 'General Aggregate Limit (Other Than Products-Completed Operations) $2,000,000.' No CG 25 03 (Per Project Aggregate) or CG 25 04 (Per Location Aggregate) is on the endorsement schedule. BOP also has CG 21 60 (Limitation of Coverage to Designated Premises or Project) — coverage is restricted to 5310 S 32nd St ONLY.
findings.gap_description: $2M general aggregate erodes across all covered events in the policy year. With CG 21 60 already restricting CGL to 5310 S 32nd St, Per Location aggregate is moot for the CGL as currently configured. BUT — if the Designated Premises restriction is removed (separate finding recommends doing so), Per Project / Per Location aggregate becomes important to preserve $2M for each subsequent loss event. Worth scheduling alongside the Designated Premises fix.
findings.plain_english: Your $2M general-aggregate limit is shared across the entire policy year — one big loss can eat up most of it, leaving the rest of the year underinsured. Today this is partly moot because the CGL is locked to one address only, but as soon as we remove that restriction (which we should), we should also add a 'Per Project Aggregate' or 'Per Location Aggregate' so each project or location has its own $2M.
findings.recommendation: Schedule CG 25 03 (Per Project Aggregate) AND/OR CG 25 04 (Per Location Aggregate) at the same time as CG 21 60 (Designated Premises) is removed. Confirm umbrella has matching follow-form aggregate, since many umbrellas do NOT — UMB-8 finding addresses umbrella side.
discoveryQuestions: How many simultaneous customer projects do you typically have running at any given time, and how many physical locations does any portion of your work touch?
If you had a $1.5M loss in March and another $1M loss in November, would you understand that today's policy might leave you with only $500K of remaining aggregate for the second one?

findings.requirement_type: Primary & Non-Contributory — CGL
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF CGL-27 — primary & non-contributory wording is required by virtually every aerospace customer purchase order and supplier MSA.
findings.policy_quote: BOP checklist 'primary_noncontributory': false. No CG 20 01 (Primary And Noncontributory — Other Insurance Condition) on the endorsement schedule. The scheduled AI endorsement CG 20 28 07 04 does not include built-in primary & non-contributory language.
findings.gap_description: CGL has no primary & non-contributory endorsement. Aerospace customers, equipment lessors, and most commercial counterparties require their AI grant to be on a primary and non-contributory basis — meaning Precision Aero's policy responds first and does NOT seek contribution from the AI's own insurance. Without CG 20 01 (or AI form with embedded P&NC), every customer that requires P&NC is left technically non-compliant. The umbrella also lacks a P&NC giveback (separate finding) — so even if an AI gets primary on the underlying, the umbrella sits bare excess.
findings.plain_english: Most of your aerospace customer purchase orders require your insurance to act 'primary and non-contributory' for them — meaning your policy pays first and doesn't ask their insurance to chip in. Your CGL doesn't have that endorsement. Every customer contract that requires this language is a contract where your policy is technically not in compliance. The fix is a standard endorsement called 'CG 20 01.'
findings.recommendation: Add CG 20 01 04 13 (Primary And Noncontributory — Other Insurance Condition) to the BOP CGL. Coordinate with Umbrella PNC follow-form fix (UMB-3 finding).
discoveryQuestions: Pull a typical customer PO — what does it say about your insurance being 'primary and non-contributory'?
When a customer asks for a certificate showing primary and non-contributory status, what's the office process today, and have we ever had to issue a non-conforming COI?

findings.requirement_type: Pollution / Total Pollution Exclusion — CGL & Umbrella + No CPL
findings.contract_quote: Aerospace machining operations use cutting fluids, coolants, solvents (often chlorinated), oil, hydraulic fluid, electroplating and surface-treatment chemicals — all of which are environmental release exposures.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.e (Pg 9) — Total Pollution Exclusion: bars BI/PD at premises owned/rented/occupied; sites used for waste handling/storage; sites where pollutants are brought on by the insured or its contractors; and governmental cleanup directives. Only carve-back: heat/smoke/fumes from a hostile fire. The base CG 00 01 also contains the standard pollution exclusion (Section I.2.f). No standalone Contractors Pollution Liability (CPL) or Premises Pollution Liability policy is in the program. Also note: Silica Exclusion CG 21 96 03 05 on the BOP — relevant to grinding/finishing dust.
findings.policy_page: Umbrella Pg 9 (I.2.e); BOP Pg 6 (CG 00 01 I.2.f); BOP CG 21 96
findings.gap_description: Both the CGL and umbrella have absolute pollution exclusions. There is no Contractors Pollution Liability (CPL) or Premises Pollution Liability (PPL) policy in the program. Aerospace machining typically generates: (a) used cutting fluids and coolant disposal exposure, (b) chlorinated solvent vapor degreaser exposure, (c) cleaning chemical and parts-washer waste, (d) potential historic contamination at the leased premises, (e) silica/respirable dust from grinding (already specifically excluded by CG 21 96), (f) hydraulic fluid and lube oil releases. A coolant-tank rupture into the storm drain, a vapor-degreaser release, an EPA inspection finding historic VOC contamination — all uninsured anywhere in the program.
findings.plain_english: Every part of your insurance program — CGL and umbrella — refuses to pay for pollution claims. There is no separate environmental policy in your program. For a machine shop with coolants, solvents, vapor degreasers, and grinding dust, that's a real exposure. A coolant-tank failure that runs into the storm drain, a chlorinated solvent vapor release, or an EPA finding of historic VOC contamination at your leased premises could each cost six or seven figures with zero insurance response. The fix is a Contractors Pollution / Premises Pollution policy.
findings.recommendation: (1) Place a combined CPL/PPL policy. (2) Limits benchmark for an aerospace machine shop: $1M each / $2M aggregate minimum, $5M aggregate preferred. (3) Confirm coverage for: gradual pollution at scheduled premises, sudden-and-accidental release, transportation pollution (cargo policy + CPL coordination), historic on-site contamination if Phase I/II environmental due diligence supports. (4) Coordinate retroactive date with environmental site assessments for the leased premises. (5) Confirm CPL responds for silica/respirable dust and is not subject to a separate silica exclusion (a common carve-out).
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through your shop's chemical inventory — what coolants, solvents, vapor degreasers, parts-washer chemistries, and surface-treatment chemicals do you use?
Has the 5310 S 32nd St property had a Phase I or Phase II environmental site assessment? Do you know if the prior tenant had any release history?
If a coolant-tank ruptured tonight and ran into the storm drain, who responds — and who pays the cleanup cost and the EPA fine?
Do you do any grinding, polishing, or finishing operations that generate respirable silica dust? Have you measured the airborne silica levels and reported under OSHA's silica standard?

findings.requirement_type: TRIA / Terrorism — Rejected (cross-program)
findings.contract_quote: Aerospace facilities and supply chains can be targets of certified acts of terrorism, particularly facilities producing components for defense primes.
findings.policy_quote: BOP IL 10 09 12 20 (Pg 31) — 'TRIA coverage REJECTED. No coverage for losses from certified acts of terrorism.' Umbrella IL 10 09 12 20 (Pg 6) — same TRIA rejection. Umbrella CU 21 35 01 15 (Pg 24) — 'Exclusion of Certified Acts of Terrorism and Exclusion of Other Acts of Terrorism Committed Outside the United States.'
findings.gap_description: Insured rejected TRIA on both BOP and Umbrella. For an aerospace shop supplying defense primes (Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop, Raytheon, etc.) the calibration of this risk is non-trivial: certified acts of terrorism targeting defense supply chain are a real threat scenario, even if low probability for a Phoenix industrial location. Confirm the insured's rejection was an informed choice — TRIA premium for an industrial premium of this size is typically modest (1-3% of CGL premium).
findings.plain_english: Your policy expressly rejects coverage for terrorism. Likely a non-issue for a Phoenix machine shop, but worth a one-minute conversation: (a) does any of your customer base ask about terrorism coverage on certificates? (b) the premium to add terrorism coverage is usually small. If you supply defense primes whose facilities have been threatened in the past, this rejection should be revisited.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with insured whether TRIA rejection was an informed decision. Re-quote terrorism premium for both BOP and Umbrella and present rejection with documented cost-benefit. If insured supplies defense primes with their own terrorism-coverage requirements, opt back in.
discoveryQuestions: Do any of your customer purchase orders ask whether you carry terrorism coverage, or list terrorism on the COI requirements?
Was the decision to reject TRIA a deliberate one, and if so, was it based on the premium dollars or because you didn't see the exposure?

findings.requirement_type: Designated Premises Limitation — CG 21 60
findings.contract_quote: RMF — CGL coverage should be unrestricted to operations the insured performs anywhere they perform them.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CG 21 60 09 98 — Limitation of Coverage to Designated Premises or Project. 'The insurance applies only to "bodily injury," "property damage," "personal and advertising injury" and medical expenses arising out of: (1) The ownership, maintenance or use of the premises shown in the Schedule and operations necessary or incidental to those premises; or (2) The project shown in the Schedule.' Schedule restricts to 5310 S 32nd St, Phoenix.
findings.policy_page: BOP Pg 6 (forms list); CG 21 60 form schedule
findings.gap_description: This is the harshest restriction on the policy. CGL responds ONLY to operations at 5310 S 32nd St, Phoenix. ANY off-premises operations are uninsured: (a) customer-site visits and meetings, (b) trade shows and aerospace conferences, (c) AOG (aircraft-on-ground) emergency support visits, (d) installation, service, or audit visits at customer plants, (e) sub-tier vendor visits, (f) parts-pickup or delivery operations not covered by Auto, (g) marketing or sales calls to primes, (h) pop-up second locations or expansion sites. For an aerospace component manufacturer, this is a critical structural defect. Combined with no HNOA confirmation (separate finding) and Products excluded entirely (separate finding), Precision Aero's CGL is an extraordinarily narrow policy.
findings.plain_english: Your CGL only works at one address — 5310 S 32nd St, Phoenix. The minute you go to a customer site, a trade show, an AOG support visit, a vendor's plant, or anywhere else, you have NO general-liability coverage. For an aerospace shop where customer-site work, sales meetings, and trade-show attendance are routine, this is one of the most restrictive endorsements I've ever seen on a policy. We should demand removal at the next renewal or shop the program to a market that doesn't impose this restriction.
findings.recommendation: (1) Demand immediate removal of CG 21 60. If Pekin refuses, treat as a placement defect and shop. (2) If keeping for now, schedule every off-premises activity Precision Aero performs and confirm whether it's incidental to the listed premises (most aerospace travel will not qualify). (3) Coordinate the per-project and per-location aggregate fix (separate finding) to be added simultaneously when CG 21 60 is removed.
discoveryQuestions: How often do you or your team go to a customer's site — Boeing, Lockheed, a tier-1 prime — for meetings, audits, AOG support, or product reviews?
Do you exhibit at trade shows like Paris Air Show, Farnborough, MRO Americas, or smaller industry conferences? Where, how often?
If a sales VP visiting a Boeing facility caused property damage at Boeing's plant tomorrow, do you understand that your CGL — restricted to 5310 S 32nd St — would not respond?

findings.requirement_type: Products-Completed Operations Hazard — EXCLUDED (CGL & Umbrella)
findings.contract_quote: An aerospace component manufacturer's products-completed operations exposure is the single largest tort exposure they face — a defective machined part causing an in-flight or ground incident is the worst-case scenario.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CGL Dec — 'Products/Completed Operations Aggregate Limit: EXCLUDED' with $0.00 advance premium. Form CG 21 04 11 85 (Exclusion - Products/Completed Operations Hazard) is on the endorsement schedule. Umbrella Dec — 'Products/Completed Operations Aggregate' shown as Excluded; the Schedule of Underlying mirrors this — underlying GL Products/Completed Ops Aggregate = EXCLUDED.
findings.policy_page: BOP Pg 6 (Dec, CG 21 04 listing); Umbrella Pg 3 (Dec)
findings.gap_description: Both the BOP CGL and the Umbrella have Products-Completed Operations Hazard ENTIRELY EXCLUDED. CG 21 04 strips the products and completed operations hazard from the CGL — the most fundamental exposure for any manufacturer is gone. The umbrella has nothing to follow form to because the underlying does not provide products coverage. For 'Precision Aero' — a name that signals aerospace component manufacturing — this is a structural catastrophe-level uninsured exposure. A defective machined part causing aircraft engine FOD, a structural failure, an in-flight emergency, or a tooling/tool-strike injury after the product leaves the shop has ZERO coverage anywhere in the program. Aerospace products-liability claims regularly run $10M–$100M+. This is the single largest finding on the program.
findings.plain_english: This is the most serious finding on your entire program. Your insurance does NOT cover claims arising from products you've shipped or work you've completed. None. Zero. The CGL specifically excludes products-completed operations and the umbrella has nothing to sit over. For an aerospace shop named 'Precision Aero,' this is the single most important coverage in the entire program — and you don't have it. A defective bracket, a mis-machined fastener, a part that fails inflight — your business is exposed personally to claims that easily reach $10M, $50M, or $100M. This must be fixed before the next aerospace PO ships.
findings.recommendation: (1) IMMEDIATE: Place a standalone Aerospace Products Liability policy or restore Products-Completed Operations on the CGL. (2) Limit benchmark: $5M minimum, $10M+ preferred for aerospace components, with umbrella attaching above. (3) Confirm coverage for: in-flight failure, ground-incident failure, FOD damage to other components, follow-on prime liability, fitness-for-purpose, engineered-to-print and design-driven claims (coordinate with Manufacturers E&O finding — many aerospace markets bundle Products + E&O). (4) Confirm grandfathering / prior acts coverage for products already in the field. (5) Until placed, treat every shipment as an uninsured catastrophe-level exposure and discuss with the insured's senior leadership immediately.
discoveryQuestions: How many parts have you shipped to aerospace customers in the last 36 months, and what's the highest-criticality application any of those parts ended up in — flight-critical, structural, engine, secondary structure?
Do your customers have you sign a 'flowdown' agreement assigning warranty and liability obligations to you for parts that go into their assemblies?

If a Precision Aero-machined bracket failed in flight tomorrow and contributed to an incident, has anyone — including the prior broker — ever told you that your current insurance doesn't cover that scenario at all?
What's the price of a single Boeing tier-1 PO — and what's the dollar value of all parts you've ever shipped to that customer that are still in service somewhere in the world?

findings.requirement_type: Silica or Silica-Related Dust Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Machining, grinding, polishing, blasting, and finishing operations on parts containing silicates can produce respirable silica dust — an OSHA-regulated occupational exposure.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CG 21 96 03 05 — 'Silica or Silica-Related Dust Exclusion.' Excludes BI/PD/Personal & Advertising Injury arising out of silica or silica-related dust.
findings.gap_description: CG 21 96 strips silica-related claims from the CGL. For a machine shop performing grinding, finishing, or working on castings/composites containing silicates, this is an exposure: (a) employee respiratory disease (handled by WC, not CGL), (b) third-party silica claims from contractors, visitors, or customers exposed during shop visits, (c) take-home silica liability theories where employees expose family members. WC handles employee respiratory claims. CGL silica exclusion specifically targets the third-party and bystander theories.
findings.plain_english: Your CGL excludes claims arising from silica dust. Employees inhaling shop dust are handled by WC. The exclusion bites for: visitors who claim respiratory illness from shop tours, family members of workers who inhale dust off work clothes, and similar third-party theories. For grinding and polishing operations these claims are real but uncommon. Worth flagging as a Bad rather than Ugly because WC catches the main employee exposure.
findings.recommendation: (1) Document grinding/finishing/polishing operations and silica-control measures. (2) If silica exposure is meaningful, place a standalone industrial-hygiene/pollution policy that responds for silica or negotiate removal of CG 21 96 (most carriers won't budge). (3) Coordinate WC for employee respiratory exposure.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: WC for employee respiratory injury; CPL/IH coverage if placed for third-party theories
discoveryQuestions: What grinding, polishing, finishing, or shot-blasting operations does the shop perform, and have you measured airborne silica levels?
Do you allow customer or visitor tours of the shop floor? Are visitors given respiratory protection?

findings.requirement_type: Wrap-Up (OCIP/CCIP) Exclusion — CGL & Umbrella
findings.contract_quote: RMF — wrap-up exclusions should be evaluated against the insured's actual exposure to OCIP/CCIP-controlled work; some forms exclude even when no wrap is in effect.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CG 40 14 12 20 — Exclusion - Designated Operations Covered by a Consolidated (Wrap-Up) Insurance Program. Umbrella CU 00 38 09 00 (Pg 4) — Schedule reads: 'Any and All Operations Performed in conjunction with a consolidated (Wrap-Up) Insurance Program' — applies regardless of whether the wrap is in effect, has adequate limits, or provides identical coverage.
findings.gap_description: Both CGL and Umbrella exclude wrap-up-covered operations. The umbrella endorsement is the harsh variant — applies even when the wrap is not in effect or has inadequate limits. For Precision Aero, the relevance depends on whether they perform any work at customer-controlled construction sites under an OCIP/CCIP. Most pure-machine-shop operations don't, but if the shop ever takes on (a) work at a customer's plant expansion site, (b) a wrap-controlled defense facility, or (c) install/integration work at a primes' site under wrap, the umbrella will sit out and the CGL will not respond either. After the wrap's tail expires, completed-ops claims are also uninsured.
findings.plain_english: If you ever do work on a customer's construction site that's under a 'wrap-up' insurance program (OCIP/CCIP — common at large defense and aerospace facility builds), your CGL and umbrella both refuse to back you up. You'd have to rely solely on the wrap policy and its tail. Probably a non-issue if you stay in your shop, but if you take on any installation, integration, or on-site work at a customer plant, this exclusion bites.
findings.recommendation: (1) Inventory any customer projects that involve on-site work or fall under a wrap. (2) For each wrap-covered project, demand a copy of the wrap binder, schedule of underlying, and tail/sunset provisions. (3) Negotiate replacement of the umbrella's harsh CU 00 38 09 00 with a less-restrictive form (excluding only when wrap is actually in effect) at next renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Do you perform any installation, integration, or on-site work at customer plants — and if so, are any of those projects under an OCIP or CCIP?
Have you ever been asked to enroll in a customer's wrap-up program for a specific project?

findings.requirement_type: Protective Safeguards Sprinkler Warranty
findings.contract_quote: RMF — Protective Safeguards endorsements suspend coverage if the warranty isn't maintained; operational discipline must match the warranty.
findings.policy_quote: BOP CP 12 10 11 85 (Pg 15) — Protective Safeguards. P-1 Automatic Sprinkler System required. Coverage automatically suspended if Insured fails to immediately notify carrier of any suspension/impairment of the protected safeguard, OR fails to maintain in working order. Sprinkler restoration must occur within 48 hours.
findings.gap_description: CP 12 10 is a coverage-killing endorsement: if the sprinkler system goes down, even briefly (e.g., for maintenance, system flush, valve work), and Pekin is not immediately notified, OR if the system isn't restored to service within 48 hours, ALL property coverage is automatically suspended. A fire during a sprinkler outage = no coverage on $11.8M of BPP. Operational discipline (notify carrier of planned shutdowns, document restoration within 48 hours, maintain inspection logs) must be airtight.
findings.plain_english: Your Property policy has a clause that says: if your sprinkler system goes down for any reason — even routine maintenance — and you don't immediately tell Pekin, OR if you don't restore service within 48 hours, your $11.8M of business personal property coverage is automatically SUSPENDED. A fire during that gap = nothing covered. We need a written facility procedure: any sprinkler outage triggers immediate notice to the broker AND documented restoration timeline.
findings.recommendation: (1) Establish written procedure: any sprinkler shutdown — planned or unplanned — triggers same-day notice to broker AND Pekin. (2) Maintain sprinkler inspection logs (NFPA 25 — quarterly/annual). (3) Confirm 48-hour restoration timeline is operationally feasible — especially if the system requires specialty parts. (4) Negotiate softening of the endorsement at renewal — many carriers offer a 30-day grace period or a notice-only requirement.
discoveryQuestions: Who handles sprinkler maintenance for your facility, and what's the inspection cadence — NFPA 25 quarterly?
If the sprinkler system needed to be drained for valve work or pipe repair, what's the typical downtime — and does anyone today notify the insurance carrier when that happens?
Is there a written procedure for sprinkler-system outages, and who at Precision Aero is responsible for executing it?

findings.requirement_type: Property Loss Settlement — ACV vs Replacement Cost Conflict
findings.contract_quote: RMF — Property loss settlement basis (ACV vs RC vs Agreed Value) must be clearly stated on the Dec page and consistent across endorsements.
findings.policy_quote: BOP IL 20 25 07 20 (Pg 35) — 'Actual Cash Value Endorsement.' Modifies BOP, Commercial Property, and Commercial Inland Marine coverage parts. Defines ACV as replacement cost less depreciation. Property Dec page: BPP marked '*** REPLACEMENT COST AND AGREED VALUE'; Building Improvement/Betterment + Legal Liability marked '*' for Replacement Cost. Per the analysis: 'Loss settlement basis should be confirmed in writing with carrier.'
findings.gap_description: Direct contradiction between Property Dec (Replacement Cost & Agreed Value) and IL 20 25 (ACV controls). Standard insurance interpretation: the more specific endorsement (IL 20 25) often controls over the Dec page schedule. If ACV applies, $11.8M BPP recovery on a total loss could be reduced by 30-60% depending on age of equipment — meaning Precision Aero might recover $5M–$8M instead of $11.8M after a fire. Aerospace machine tools (CNC mills, lathes, EDMs, CMMs) depreciate aggressively on books even when fair market value remains high. The ambiguity is unacceptable; written carrier confirmation is required IMMEDIATELY.
findings.plain_english: Your Property dec page says you have $11.8M of equipment coverage on a 'replacement cost and agreed value' basis — meaning Pekin would pay full replacement cost without depreciation. But buried at page 35 is an endorsement that says coverage is on 'actual cash value' — replacement cost MINUS depreciation. After a fire, depreciation on machine tools could cut your recovery from $11.8M to as low as $5M–$8M. This contradiction has to be resolved in writing with Pekin BEFORE a loss happens. Otherwise you're betting which clause a court will enforce.
findings.recommendation: (1) IMMEDIATE: Demand written confirmation from Pekin which loss settlement basis applies — Replacement Cost (Dec page) or ACV (IL 20 25). (2) Insist on Replacement Cost — and have Pekin remove or amend IL 20 25 to apply only to specifically scheduled items not on the BPP. (3) If carrier insists on ACV, re-quantify equipment values on a depreciated basis and re-set BPP limit accordingly — OR shop to a carrier that will write Replacement Cost without ACV override. (4) Update Agreed Value statement annually with equipment list.
discoveryQuestions: What's the book value of your CNC equipment, EDMs, CMMs, and shop tooling versus the cost to replace them new today? Is there a 30-50% gap?
After a total fire loss tonight, would you expect Pekin to pay you the cost to replace the equipment new — or the depreciated 'book' value?
Has anyone — Pekin, the prior broker, or anyone — ever explained the IL 20 25 ACV endorsement and the contradiction with the Dec page?

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine Cyber Exclusion (Motor Transit Cargo)
findings.contract_quote: RMF — Inland Marine cargo coverage should respond to cyber-triggered cargo loss (e.g., GPS spoofing, hacked dispatch, stolen via electronic means).
findings.policy_quote: BOP CM 75 03 02 21 (Pg 27) — Cyber Incident Exclusion (Inland Marine). Excludes IM cargo coverage for unauthorized access, malicious code, or denial of service attacks. Resulting fire/explosion exception only.
findings.gap_description: Motor Transit Cargo $320K limit on the 2018 Dodge Ram excludes cyber-triggered cargo events. If GPS spoofing redirects a load, if dispatch credentials are stolen and a load misdirected, or if a hacked routing system results in cargo loss, IM does not respond (only resulting fire/explosion is). For aerospace cargo where individual parts can be valued at 5-6 figures, the cyber-triggered cargo loss risk is real. Coordinate with Cyber Liability finding — a properly placed Cyber policy with first-party cargo extension can address.
findings.plain_english: Your $320K cargo policy on the truck won't pay if cargo is stolen, redirected, or lost because someone hacked your dispatch, spoofed GPS, or otherwise manipulated electronic systems. Aerospace cargo theft is targeted — high-value, easy-to-resell parts. A cyber-triggered cargo loss has no insurance response. Fold this into the broader Cyber Liability placement.
findings.recommendation: Address through standalone Cyber Liability placement (separate finding) — confirm cyber policy includes first-party cargo / property-in-transit cyber-triggered loss extension. Alternatively negotiate removal of CM 75 03 with carrier (often a hard no).
discoveryQuestions: Do you ship aerospace parts — even via your one truck — that have street resale value? Has cargo theft ever been a concern?
How is your dispatch and shipping data secured today, and has anyone walked through the cyber-supply-chain attack scenarios?

findings.requirement_type: Care, Custody and Control — Property Of Others on Premises (Property side)
findings.contract_quote: RMF — Property Of Others coverage on the Property side responds to first-party loss to customer-supplied property at insured's premises.
findings.policy_quote: BOP Property limits — 'Personal Property of Others $1,500,000.'
findings.gap_description: $1.5M Personal Property of Others on the Property side covers first-party physical-damage exposure to customer property at the premises (fire, water, theft, etc.). This is a meaningful coverage but does NOT close the CGL Care, Custody and Control liability gap (separate finding) — the $1.5M responds to property-level losses; CCC bailee LIABILITY for damage caused by Precision Aero's negligence is a separate exposure.
findings.plain_english: Good news on this one: your Property policy includes $1.5M for customer-owned property kept at your shop — that responds for fire, theft, or water damage to a customer's part on your floor. It does NOT replace a Bailee policy for damage you caused to customer property (separate finding above) — those are different coverages — but it's a meaningful piece of the puzzle and worth crediting.
findings.recommendation: Confirm $1.5M sublimit is adequate against highest-value customer property on premises. Coordinate with Bailee placement (separate CCC finding) so that first-party (Property) and third-party-liability (Bailee) work together.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Other Insurance / Primary & Non-Contributory Follow-Form
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-3 — umbrella's 'other insurance' clause must coordinate with underlying primary and non-contributory endorsements.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section IV.9 — bare excess over underlying and any other collectible insurance; no Primary & Non-Contributory giveback. Per analysis: 'If the underlying GL is endorsed PNC for an AI, the umbrella will NOT follow that endorsement and will sit excess of any other valid and collectible insurance — a classic conditional-follow-form gap.'
findings.gap_description: Even if the underlying CGL is endorsed CG 20 01 (Primary And Noncontributory) for additional insureds, the umbrella's bare-excess Other Insurance clause does NOT follow form to that grant. So: AI customer suffers a $3M loss, underlying $1M responds primary, but the umbrella seeks contribution from the AI's own $5M umbrella — defeating the customer's contractual expectation that Precision Aero's coverage is primary all the way up. Classic conditional-follow-form trap that breaks customer contracts at the umbrella level.
findings.plain_english: Even if we add a 'primary and non-contributory' endorsement to your CGL (which we should — separate finding), the umbrella above it has its own clause that says the umbrella will look for contribution from the customer's own insurance once losses go above $1M. Your customer's contract said your insurance is primary all the way up — but the umbrella will fight that at the back end. The fix is a follow-form PNC giveback on the umbrella, OR scheduling a primary-and-noncontributory endorsement on the umbrella itself.
findings.recommendation: Request umbrella endorsement adding follow-form Primary & Non-Contributory or a standalone PNC giveback on the umbrella for any AI for whom the underlying is endorsed PNC. Coordinate with CGL CG 20 01 (separate finding). Several carriers offer this as a no-cost endorsement.
discoveryQuestions: When a customer demands 'primary and non-contributory' status, does that requirement extend up through the umbrella in their PO language?
If a $3M claim hit and the umbrella tried to share with your customer's own carrier above the first $1M, do you understand that's a contract breach with that customer?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Waiver of Subrogation Follow-Form
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-3(2) — Transfer of Rights of Recovery / Waiver of Subrogation must follow form to underlying.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section IV.8 — standard subrogation language; no Waiver of Subrogation giveback. Per analysis: 'If the underlying carries a blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement, the umbrella does NOT follow form to that waiver.'
findings.gap_description: Umbrella has no follow-form Waiver of Subrogation giveback. Even if the underlying CGL is endorsed CG 24 04 (Blanket Waiver), the umbrella retains subrogation rights against parties Precision Aero contractually agreed to waive against. Above the underlying limit, Pekin Umbrella can sue customers — defeating the customer relationship and breaching the indemnity in Precision Aero's customer agreements at the umbrella layer.
findings.plain_english: Even after we add a blanket waiver of subrogation to your CGL (separate finding), the umbrella above it can still sue your customers to recover money paid above the first $1M. Your customer contracts say your INSURANCE — primary AND umbrella — won't sue them. The umbrella needs a matching follow-form waiver giveback.
findings.recommendation: Request umbrella endorsement adding follow-form Waiver of Subrogation, or a standalone blanket Waiver of Subrogation giveback on the umbrella matching the underlying CG 24 04.
discoveryQuestions: If the umbrella sued one of your top aerospace customers to recover a paid claim, what does that do to the contractual indemnity Precision Aero owes that customer under the supplier agreement?
Have you ever discussed with Pekin whether their umbrella's subrogation provision matches the waiver on your CGL?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Conditional Follow Form / AI Status
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-4 — additional insured status on the umbrella should be at least as broad as the underlying.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section II.6 — AI follow-form for 'any other person or organization who is an Insured under the underlying insurance,' but expressly limited to 'no broader than that of the underlying insurance.' Section I.1.b(1) caps payment at the part of ultimate net loss exceeding underlying limits.
findings.gap_description: Conditional follow-form umbrella with the well-known 'no broader than the underlying' limitation. Combined with: (a) underlying CGL having only narrow scheduled AI grants (no blanket), (b) underlying GL having Products-Completed Ops EXCLUDED, (c) underlying CGL Designated Premises restriction CG 21 60. Every AI granted on the underlying is similarly narrow on the umbrella. Umbrella does not broaden, does not give P&NC where underlying doesn't, does not extend AI status to entities not on the underlying.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella's 'follow form' for additional insureds is conditional — it can only be as broad as the underlying CGL. Since the underlying CGL only schedules four AIs (Makino, Black Mountain Aerospace, Wells Fargo, Zions) and has no blanket AI, the umbrella has the same four AIs. The fix is fixing the underlying first (separate Blanket AI finding), then ensuring the umbrella's follow-form correctly picks up those new AI grants.
findings.recommendation: Address through CGL Blanket AI placement (separate finding). After CG 20 33 / CG 20 37 are added underlying, confirm the umbrella's Section II.6 picks up those grants automatically. Verify with Pekin in writing that umbrella will follow form to a future blanket-AI underlying without needing separate AI scheduling on the umbrella.
discoveryQuestions: When a customer requires AI status on both the primary and umbrella — does our COI process today reflect that the umbrella follow-form depends on the underlying being correctly endorsed?
Has any customer ever rejected your COI because the AI grant didn't show on both the CGL and umbrella lines?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Defense Costs Outside Limits
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-5 — Supplementary Payments / Defense should be in addition to (outside) the limit of liability.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.3 — Supplementary Payments are payable IN ADDITION to the limit of insurance.
findings.gap_description: Defense and supplementary payments are outside the umbrella limit when the umbrella defends. Standard market favorable construction. Note: per analysis, 'the umbrella only has a duty to defend when no underlying applies or underlying aggregate has been exhausted by paid losses' — typical conditional-follow-form behavior.
findings.plain_english: Good news: when your umbrella has to defend a claim, the defense costs come out of a separate bucket from the $5M policy limit. So a long, expensive defense won't eat into the indemnity available for a settlement or judgment. This is the favorable construction.
findings.recommendation: No change. Confirm clients understand defense-outside-limits applies only when the umbrella is defending (i.e., underlying is exhausted or doesn't apply); routine claims are defended by the underlying with underlying-form treatment of defense costs.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Maintenance of Underlying
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-6 — failure to maintain underlying should not invalidate the umbrella; instead the umbrella should respond as if underlying were in force.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section IV.10 — favorable wording: failure to maintain does NOT invalidate the umbrella; policy applies as though underlying were in force at scheduled limits.
findings.gap_description: Favorable Maintenance of Underlying wording — the umbrella does not lose all coverage if underlying lapses or reduces. Instead, the umbrella treats underlying as if still in place at scheduled limits — i.e., the insured bears the gap (no drop-down) but the umbrella remains in force. This is the better of the two common variants. Worth confirming insured understands they still bear the gap if underlying lapses.
findings.plain_english: Good news: if for any reason the underlying CGL or Auto policy lapsed mid-term (carrier insolvency, missed payment), your umbrella does NOT disappear. The umbrella still works — it just acts as if the underlying were still in place at the original $1M, meaning Precision Aero personally would have to fund the first $1M of any loss. The umbrella stays in force. This is the favorable version of this clause.
findings.recommendation: No change. Confirm insured operationally understands: maintain the underlying premiums on time and at the scheduled limits; if underlying ever lapses or reduces, the umbrella does not drop down to fill the gap.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Notice & Knowledge
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-7 — umbrella notice obligation should be limited to person responsible for insurance.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section IV.6 — broad 'you must see to it that we... are notified as soon as practicable' language with no carve-back limiting knowledge to the person responsible for insurance.
findings.gap_description: Umbrella's notice obligation matches the underlying's broad ISO wording — any employee's knowledge can be imputed. Addressed through the Notice & Knowledge fix on the underlying (separate finding); umbrella will inherit through follow-form once underlying is endorsed. If carrier won't endorse the underlying, request a parallel endorsement on the umbrella.
findings.plain_english: Same issue as the underlying CGL/Auto/EL — any employee's knowledge of an occurrence can trigger the notice clock at the umbrella level. Fix on the underlying first; umbrella follows form. If for some reason the underlying can't be fixed, ask Pekin to put a Notice & Knowledge giveback on the umbrella directly.
findings.recommendation: Address via underlying Notice & Knowledge endorsement (separate finding). If umbrella does not pick up through follow-form, request standalone N&K endorsement on the umbrella.
discoveryQuestions: Same as the underlying N&K finding — if a shop-floor employee's knowledge of an incident is imputed to the company at the underlying, does the umbrella's same broad language compound the timing risk?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Per Project / Per Location Aggregate Follow-Form
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-8 — many umbrellas do not have a follow-form aggregate, which can be problematic when contracts require it.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella has no per-project or per-location aggregate giveback noted in the analysis. Standard CU 00 01 form does not automatically follow form on aggregates of this type.
findings.gap_description: Even after Per Project / Per Location aggregate is endorsed on the underlying CGL (separate finding), the umbrella does NOT automatically follow form on those aggregate structures. Multiple losses can erode the umbrella's $5M aggregate even when the underlying has them split per project. Address only after the underlying CGL aggregate fix is in place — and verify whether the umbrella will follow form or needs a separate per-project / per-location aggregate endorsement.
findings.plain_english: After we add 'per project aggregate' to your CGL, the umbrella above it doesn't automatically have the same structure. Multiple losses across multiple projects all eat from the umbrella's $5M total. We should ask Pekin to mirror the underlying's per-project structure on the umbrella — most carriers will, but it's not automatic.
findings.recommendation: Request umbrella endorsement adding per-project and per-location aggregate matching the underlying. Confirm in writing.
discoveryQuestions: If you had two or three significant claims in one policy year across multiple customer projects, would you understand that today the umbrella's $5M aggregate is shared across all of them?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Professional Liability Excluded
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-9 — umbrella should provide a means-and-methods giveback for professional liability or be broader than primary.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.g — Professional Liability Exclusion: '"professional liability,"' broadly defined in V.15 (engineers, architects, surveyors, draftsmen explicitly listed). No means-and-methods giveback.
findings.gap_description: Umbrella replicates the underlying's professional services exclusion with no carve-back for means-and-methods (i.e., negligence in the manner of performing physical work). For an aerospace machine shop, even if Manufacturers E&O is placed (separate finding), the umbrella has no means-and-methods giveback — meaning means-and-methods ambiguity at claim could fall into the professional-services exclusion and never reach umbrella indemnity. A standalone Manufacturers E&O policy (or excess E&O above the standalone) is required to fill the umbrella gap.
findings.plain_english: Even if we place a separate Manufacturers E&O policy (separate finding), the umbrella above the CGL still excludes professional services entirely — there's no excess umbrella sitting over E&O claims. So your E&O policy stands alone at its own limit. We should evaluate whether Excess E&O is appropriate to layer on top of the primary E&O for catastrophic-aerospace exposure.
findings.recommendation: Address by placing standalone Manufacturers E&O (separate finding) at adequate primary limits ($5M+). Optionally place Excess E&O over the primary to layer up. Do NOT rely on the Pekin umbrella to backstop E&O — it won't.
discoveryQuestions: If your professional services exposure is $10M+ in a worst-case design-defect claim, are you comfortable that a standalone $2M E&O alone is enough — or should we be layering excess E&O above it?
Have you ever priced excess Manufacturers E&O capacity in the aerospace market?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Punitive Damages
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-10 — umbrella should not exclude punitive damages where state law permits insurance for them.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 21 36 01 15 (Pg 26) — 'Exclusion of Punitive Damages Related to a Certified Act of Terrorism' — narrowly excludes punitives only from certified terrorism. No broad punitive damages exclusion is identified in the analysis. The base CU 00 01 form does not contain an across-the-board punitive damages exclusion.
findings.gap_description: Only narrow terrorism-punitive exclusion is identified — base umbrella appears to permit punitive damages within ultimate net loss subject to state law and most-favored-jurisdiction principles. Worth confirming in writing whether Pekin's CU 00 01 base form expressly defines 'damages' to include punitive damages where insurable, and whether Arizona allows insurance of punitive damages (AZ generally does not allow direct punitive insurance for the wrongdoer's intentional conduct, but does allow vicarious punitive coverage). This is a state-law and policy-language question that warrants written carrier confirmation.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella excludes punitive damages only when they're tied to a certified terrorism event. For other cases, whether punitive damages are covered depends on (a) policy language and (b) Arizona law on insuring punitives. Arizona generally doesn't let you insure your own intentional bad conduct's punitives, but vicarious punitive damages (where you're punished for an employee's bad act) are usually insurable. We should get written carrier confirmation of how Pekin handles punitives.
findings.recommendation: Request written carrier confirmation: (a) whether Pekin's umbrella treats punitive damages as 'damages' under the base form; (b) confirmation Pekin will pay punitives where state law permits (most-favored-jurisdiction wording or 'where insurable by law'). If carrier balks, this becomes a Bad finding.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Right and Duty When Underlying Exhausted
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-11 — umbrella should have right and duty to defend when underlying limits are exhausted.
findings.policy_quote: Per analysis: 'the umbrella only has a duty to defend when no underlying applies or underlying aggregate has been exhausted by paid losses.' Section I.3 supplementary payments paid in addition to limits when umbrella defends.
findings.gap_description: Standard market construction — duty to defend triggers when underlying is exhausted by PAID losses (not just reserves). Confirms the umbrella will assume defense after the $1M underlying is exhausted, with defense outside limits. Standard expected behavior.
findings.plain_english: Good news: when the underlying $1M is paid out, the umbrella picks up defense as well as indemnity, with defense costs outside the umbrella limit. Standard, expected, correct construction.
findings.recommendation: No change. Confirm insured understands 'paid losses' (not 'reserved') is the trigger — the umbrella does not assume defense early.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Total Pollution Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-12 — total pollution exclusion bars even sudden-and-accidental release coverage; no givebacks under endorsement.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.e — Absolute Total Pollution Exclusion. Only carve-back: heat/smoke/fumes from a hostile fire.
findings.gap_description: Address through CPL placement (separate finding). Note: even after CPL is placed at primary, the umbrella above does NOT follow form to CPL because (a) CPL is not a scheduled underlying line, (b) Pekin umbrella has its own absolute pollution exclusion. CPL must carry its own adequate primary limit OR Excess Pollution must be placed.
findings.plain_english: The umbrella's pollution exclusion is even harsher than the CGL's. After we place a primary CPL/PPL policy (separate finding), the umbrella above it doesn't extend the pollution coverage — Pekin's umbrella has its own pollution exclusion and isn't going to drop the wall down. So the CPL policy stands at its own limit, or we place Excess Pollution above it.
findings.recommendation: Place primary CPL with adequate limit ($1M-$5M) AND consider Excess Pollution layer if exposure justifies. Do not rely on Pekin Umbrella to extend pollution coverage.
discoveryQuestions: After we set up primary CPL, is your worst-case environmental exposure (e.g., chlorinated solvent release at the leased premises with EPA cleanup) likely to exceed $1M-$2M?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Schedule of Underlying Completeness
findings.contract_quote: Broker RMF UMB-13 — all underlying policies must be scheduled to receive umbrella excess attachment.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella Schedule of Underlying lists: Pekin GL 006206676; Pekin Auto $1M CSL; Pekin Employers Liability 005211944. Per analysis, NOT listed: Professional Liability, Cyber Liability, Foreign Liability, Liquor Liability, Pollution Liability.
