findings.gap_description: Once standalone E&O, Cyber, EPLI, CPL, Products, etc. are placed (separate findings), they must EITHER be scheduled as underlying to the Pekin umbrella for excess attachment OR be self-sufficient on their own primary limits. Pekin's umbrella conditional follow form means new lines won't get umbrella excess unless they're scheduled AND the umbrella's exclusions don't bar them (umbrella PL exclusion, cyber exclusion, pollution exclusion, etc. block these lines from umbrella excess regardless). Practically: the umbrella will excess GL/Auto/EL only — and standalone E&O, Cyber, EPLI, CPL must each carry their own primary limits adequate to the worst-case exposure.
findings.plain_english: Once we place standalone E&O, Cyber, EPLI, and CPL policies, your $5M Pekin umbrella WILL NOT extend to those new lines. The umbrella has built-in exclusions for professional liability, cyber, and pollution — so those lines stand alone on their own primary limits. This means each new policy needs to be sized for the worst-case loss, not relying on the umbrella above it. We should look at carriers that offer umbrellas extending over E&O / Cyber if those exposures are large.
findings.recommendation: (1) Size each new standalone line (E&O, Cyber, EPLI, CPL) to be self-sufficient at adequate primary limits given umbrella will not excess them. (2) Evaluate whether to replace Pekin umbrella with an umbrella that DOES extend over E&O / Cyber / Pollution. (3) Schedule any qualifying new line on the Pekin Schedule of Underlying at next renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Looking at the new standalone policies we'd recommend (E&O, Cyber, EPLI), have you considered an umbrella structure that would extend over those lines instead of the current GL/Auto/EL-only umbrella?
What's the appetite for a higher umbrella limit — $10M, $15M — given the aerospace products exposure?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Aircraft Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Aerospace operations — even when limited to component machining — regularly involve interaction with aircraft (test flights, deliveries, hangar movements, ferry operations).
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.h(1) (Pg 10) — Aircraft Exclusion: 'BI/PD arising out of ownership, maintenance, operation, use, loading/unloading, or entrustment to others of aircraft owned by any insured or chartered without crew.'
findings.gap_description: For 'Precision Aero Inc' the aircraft exclusion is non-trivial. If Precision Aero (a) owns or leases any aircraft for company use, (b) charters an aircraft without crew, (c) handles aircraft on a ramp during delivery of components, (d) operates within a hangar where aircraft are present — the umbrella has zero coverage for any related BI/PD. Standalone Aircraft / Aviation Liability is the only response. This combines with the no-Products coverage finding to magnify aerospace-context exposure.
findings.plain_english: If Precision Aero owns, leases, or charters any aircraft — or if your operations involve handling aircraft on a ramp, in a hangar, or during delivery — your umbrella has a hard exclusion. We need to confirm: do you own any aircraft for company travel? Do you charter? Do your delivery operations ever touch an aircraft? If yes to any, an Aviation Liability policy is needed.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm whether Precision Aero owns, leases, charters, or operationally handles aircraft. (2) If yes, place standalone Aviation Liability with appropriate limits. (3) If no, document the non-exposure for file. (4) Be cautious of customer-site delivery operations where ramp/hangar exposure exists.
discoveryQuestions: Does Precision Aero own, lease, or charter any aircraft for company use, deliveries, or executive travel?
When you deliver finished parts to a customer, do your employees ever go onto a ramp, into a hangar, or near aircraft during the delivery?
Do customer-site visits ever require employees to be inside operational hangars, around AOG aircraft, or on aprons?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Discrimination Exclusion (no EPLI excess)
findings.contract_quote: RMF — umbrella should follow form to underlying EPLI (where placed) for excess attachment of EPLI losses.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.f (Pg 9) — 'Any alleged or actual discrimination by an insured against any person.'
findings.gap_description: Once a standalone EPLI policy is placed (separate finding), the Pekin umbrella does NOT excess EPLI — its discrimination exclusion bars umbrella attachment over EPLI losses. EPLI must therefore stand at its own primary limit; if the EPLI primary is exceeded, no umbrella backstop exists.
findings.plain_english: Even after we place a separate EPLI policy, your Pekin umbrella refuses to sit excess of it — the umbrella has a hard exclusion for any discrimination claim. So the EPLI policy stands alone. We need to size the EPLI limit for the worst-case wage-and-hour or harassment class-action — not rely on the umbrella behind it.
findings.recommendation: (1) Size EPLI primary limit to absorb worst-case loss. (2) Optionally place excess EPLI if exposure justifies. (3) Do not rely on Pekin umbrella behind EPLI.
discoveryQuestions: What's your worst-case wage-and-hour class-action exposure given your headcount and pay structure — could a single class action exceed $1M?
Should we be evaluating excess EPLI capacity given the umbrella won't sit over a primary EPLI?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — ERISA / Fiduciary Liability Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: RMF — umbrella should not silently exclude fiduciary liability where benefits administration creates exposure.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.k (Pg 10) — Excludes fiduciary liability arising from employee benefit plans, ERISA, Pension Reform Act.
findings.gap_description: Umbrella excludes ERISA / fiduciary exposure. Underlying BOP has EBL E&O at $1M each / $3M aggregate, but the umbrella does NOT sit excess over it. EBL is benefits-administration coverage; true Fiduciary Liability (covering plan trustees, plan-asset management, prohibited transactions) is a separate line not in the program. Recommend evaluating whether a standalone Fiduciary Liability policy is appropriate given employee benefits and any 401(k) or pension exposure.
findings.plain_english: Your benefits-administration coverage (EBL) on the BOP has $1M / $3M, but the umbrella refuses to sit excess of it. So if you have a $2M ERISA fiduciary lawsuit, the umbrella doesn't help. A separate Fiduciary Liability policy is the standard fix for plan-trustee exposure (different from EBL — Fiduciary covers trustees and plan-asset management).
findings.recommendation: (1) Evaluate whether a standalone Fiduciary Liability policy is warranted (typically yes if 401(k), pension, or significant health benefits exist). (2) Confirm EBL retroactive date issue (separate finding). (3) Do not rely on umbrella above EBL.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: EBL on BOP (limited; no umbrella excess); standalone Fiduciary policy recommended
discoveryQuestions: Do you sponsor a 401(k) or other employee benefits plan? Who are the plan trustees and fiduciaries?
Have you been advised about Fiduciary Liability insurance, separate from your benefits-administration EBL coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Insured-vs-Insured Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: RMF — Insured-vs-Insured exclusion bars cross-suits between affiliated entities.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.q (Pg 10) — 'Bars any claim brought "by or on behalf of you or any additional Named Insured."' Cross-suits between affiliated entities listed on the umbrella receive no coverage.
findings.gap_description: Today only Precision Aero Inc is named — IvI exclusion is moot. Becomes material when (a) Broad Form Named Insured is added (separate finding) bringing additional entities under the program, or (b) JV partners are scheduled. Worth flagging when the BFNI fix is implemented.
findings.plain_english: Right now you only have one named entity, so this exclusion is dormant. It activates the moment we add affiliates or JV partners — they couldn't sue each other under this umbrella. Something to keep in mind when we expand the named insured list.
findings.recommendation: Tag for revisit when Broad Form NI endorsement is added (separate finding). Confirm IvI exclusion does not bar legitimate cross-claims between affiliates.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Watercraft Exclusion (50ft+)
findings.contract_quote: RMF — watercraft exclusions should be evaluated against operations.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella CU 00 01 08 22 Section I.2.h(2) (Pg 10) — Excludes watercraft over 50 feet; under 50ft is covered only if covered by underlying and 'no broader than the underlying.'
findings.gap_description: N/A for a Phoenix landlocked aerospace machine shop. Confirmed for completeness.
findings.plain_english: N/A — no watercraft exposure for an inland aerospace shop.
findings.recommendation: No action.

findings.requirement_type: Missing Policy — Cyber Liability
findings.contract_quote: Aerospace contractors with ITAR/CUI data, CMMC obligations, and ERP/CNC dependence have severe cyber exposure not covered by general liability policies.
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Cyber Liability policy in the program. CGL CG 29 26, IM CM 75 03, and Umbrella CU 00 56 all carry absolute cyber exclusions.
findings.gap_description: See finding-011 (Cyber Excluded + No Standalone Cyber). Recorded here as a missing-policy finding for program-completeness tracking.
findings.plain_english: Repeats finding-011: no Cyber Liability policy in your program — this is the second-largest uninsured exposure after Products-Completed Operations.
findings.recommendation: See finding-011 recommendation. Place standalone Cyber Liability with $2M-$5M limits and aerospace-appropriate coverages.
discoveryQuestions: See discovery questions on finding-011.

findings.requirement_type: Missing Policy — Directors & Officers / Management Liability
findings.contract_quote: Owners and officers of a closely held manufacturer face personal exposure to claims from employees, customers, vendors, regulatory agencies, and minority shareholders.
findings.policy_quote: No D&O or Management Liability policy in this program.
findings.gap_description: No D&O / Management Liability coverage in the program. For Precision Aero (closely-held C-corp): owners/officers face personal exposure to (a) employee claims for breach of fiduciary duty in HR/benefits decisions, (b) vendor or customer claims alleging mismanagement, (c) regulatory investigations (DCMA, DCAA, OFAC, ITAR, EPA, OSHA), (d) minority shareholder claims if any non-controlling interests exist, (e) buy/sell or M&A-related claims. CGL doesn't cover. Umbrella has IvI exclusion. Without D&O, owners' personal assets are exposed.
findings.plain_english: There's no policy in your program covering you and your fellow officers personally. As an owner of a closely-held manufacturer, you face personal lawsuits from regulators (ITAR, OSHA, EPA), employees alleging mismanagement, vendors, even minority partners. Defense costs for a single regulatory investigation easily run $250K-$500K, and judgments can hit personal assets. A D&O / Management Liability policy is the standard fix — usually $1M-$2M is enough for a private aerospace shop.
findings.recommendation: Place standalone Management Liability or Private Company D&O policy. Minimum $1M each claim / $1M aggregate, ideally a packaged ML form including D&O + EPLI (separate finding) + Fiduciary (separate finding) + Crime (separate finding) — common bundling at this revenue tier.
discoveryQuestions: Who are the officers and directors of Precision Aero today, and is there any non-employee or minority shareholder in the cap table?
Have you ever been the subject of a DCMA, DCAA, ITAR, OSHA, or EPA inquiry — and if not, are you aware that defense costs for those investigations can hit six figures personally?
If a vendor sued you personally as an officer alleging fraudulent inducement or mismanagement, who pays your lawyer?

findings.requirement_type: Missing Policy — Crime / Fidelity
findings.contract_quote: Manufacturers face employee theft, funds-transfer fraud, social engineering / impersonation fraud, and forgery exposures not covered by Property or CGL policies.
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Crime / Fidelity policy identified in this program.
findings.gap_description: No Crime/Fidelity policy in the program. Common manufacturer exposures uninsured: (a) Employee theft (cash, inventory, scrap revenue, tooling), (b) funds-transfer fraud (compromised banking credentials), (c) social engineering / impersonation fraud (CEO-spoof wire requests, vendor-impersonation invoice fraud), (d) forgery or alteration of signed instruments, (e) computer fraud. For aerospace machine shops where individual parts are high-value and scrap titanium has substantial street value, employee-theft exposure is real. Social-engineering wire fraud is a top-3 SMB loss type. Coordinate with Cyber finding — many cyber policies offer social engineering sublimits but Crime is the primary line.
findings.plain_english: No coverage anywhere in your program for: employee theft, social engineering wire fraud (someone impersonates a vendor and you wire them $200K), or banking-credential fraud. For an aerospace shop with high-value parts, valuable tooling, and titanium scrap that has a real resale market, employee-theft alone is a real exposure. Social-engineering wire fraud is one of the most common losses small manufacturers suffer today. A Crime / Fidelity policy with $250K-$500K of social-engineering sublimit is the standard fix.
findings.recommendation: Place Crime / Fidelity / Commercial Crime policy. Include: (a) Employee Theft $250K-$500K, (b) Forgery/Alteration $100K, (c) Computer Fraud $250K, (d) Social Engineering / Fraudulent Funds Transfer $250K-$500K (often a sublimit), (e) Client Property coverage for customer property loss to employee theft. Coordinate sublimits with Cyber policy social-engineering coverage to avoid overlap.
discoveryQuestions: How many employees have access to the bank, payables, payroll, or vendor-master data? What are the controls on wire transfers?
If a fraudster impersonated a regular vendor and emailed updated bank instructions for an upcoming payment, would your AP team catch it before sending the wire?
What's the value of titanium and other high-grade scrap that leaves your shop in a typical month — and who manages the scrap revenue?
Has Precision Aero ever experienced employee theft, even small-dollar?

findings.requirement_type: Missing Policy — Bailee / Property of Others Liability
findings.contract_quote: Aerospace machine shops routinely receive customer-supplied tooling and parts (CFE) creating bailee liability exposure not covered by CGL or Property.
findings.policy_quote: See finding-008 (CCC exclusion + $1.5M Property Of Others is first-party only). No standalone Bailee policy in the program.
findings.gap_description: Cross-references finding-008 — captured here as a missing-policy finding for completeness. Customer property in transit, at sub-tier vendors, or post-shipment but pre-customer-acceptance has no liability response.

Beyond the cosmetics: any sister entity (a property LLC, a holding company, a related operating entity) is not automatically covered without a Broad Form Named Insured endorsement.
findings.recommendation: Have Pekin (a) correct the Form of Business field on the Dec to reflect 'Corporation', (b) remove CA 99 17 unless an individual is actually intended as a Named Insured, and (c) add a Broad Form Named Insured endorsement extending automatic coverage to subsidiaries / affiliates / related entities Precision Aero owns or controls.

A choice, not a defect, but the producer should walk Bogdan and Precision Aero through it.

findings.requirement_type: Cross-Program First Named Insured Entity Type Inconsistency (Inc vs Corp vs Unspecified)
findings.contract_quote: N/A — no upstream contract loaded; finding is structural across the program.
findings.policy_quote: BOP First Named Insured Form of Business: 'Corp'. USLI EPLI Form of Business: 'Inc'. WC PEKIN 24 Form of Business: 'Inc'. AUTO Form of Business: unspecified. UMBRELLA Form of Business: unspecified.
findings.gap_description: The five program policies disagree on the First Named Insured form-of-business field. BOP carries 'Corp,' USLI EPLI and WC PEKIN 24 carry 'Inc,' and AUTO and UMBRELLA leave the field unspecified. The human-readable name 'Precision Aero Inc' is consistent across all five, but the legal-form attribute is not. Per GAP-01 EXPANDED and GAP-20, an entity-type mismatch persisting across 3+ program policies is a systemic identification defect — a defense attorney can argue at a contested claim that the policies do not all refer to the same legal person, opening avenues for a denial or coordination-of-coverage dispute.
findings.plain_english: Your five policies don't agree on what your company actually IS. Two say 'Inc,' one says 'Corp,' and two leave it blank. It's almost certainly the same legal entity behind all five — but in a contested claim, that small documentary mismatch is exactly the kind of thread a defense lawyer pulls on to delay or deny coverage. Easy to fix today. Expensive to fix at claim time.
findings.recommendation: Pull Precision Aero's articles of incorporation and tax filings to confirm the precise legal form (C-corp, S-corp, or LLC). Then have each carrier issue an endorsement standardizing the Form-of-Business field across all five policies to match. The AUTO and UMBRELLA blank fields should be filled in with the same value as the BOP/EPLI/WC.
discoveryQuestions: Has Precision Aero ever changed its legal structure — for example, converted from an Inc to an LLC, or restructured into an S-corp? If so, when, and which policies were updated to reflect that?
When you receive a new policy or renewal, who at Precision Aero reviews the Named Insured and Form-of-Business fields against your incorporation documents — and how often does that catch a mismatch?

If a customer or vendor sued Precision Aero tomorrow and your defense counsel had to prove which legal entity was insured under each policy, would your articles of incorporation and the five Dec pages tell a single consistent story?

findings.requirement_type: Cross-Policy Additional Insured Gap — Makino Inc / Black Mountain Aerospace not specifically scheduled on Umbrella
findings.contract_quote: N/A — entity matrix evidence: Makino Inc / Black Mountain Aerospace AI on BOP only via CG 20 28 07 04 (Pg. 21).
findings.policy_quote: BOP CG 20 28 07 04 (Pg. 21) schedules 'Makino Inc, Black Mountain Aerospace' as Additional Insured. UMBRELLA Section II.6 (Pg. 11, CU 00 01 08 22): 'Any other person or organization who is an Insured under the underlying insurance' — automatic follow-form AI clause only; no scheduled AI endorsement specifying Makino.
findings.policy_page: Pg. 11 (Section II.6 — Who Is An Insured)
findings.gap_description: Makino Inc and Black Mountain Aerospace are scheduled Additional Insureds on the BOP CGL via CG 20 28 07 04 (Pg. 21) but are not specifically scheduled on the $5M Umbrella. The Umbrella's automatic AI clause (CU 00 01 08 22 Section II.6) extends coverage by reference: 'Any other person or organization who is an Insured under the underlying insurance.' This conditional follow-form likely picks Makino up — but it is conditional on the underlying AI status holding up. If the underlying AI endorsement is challenged, scope-disputed, or determined inapplicable to a particular claim, the Umbrella drops away with it. A scheduled Umbrella AI endorsement provides cleaner evidence in claim litigation. Combined limit available to Makino as AI today: $1M GL primary + $5M Umbrella = $6M, contingent on the conditional follow-form.
findings.plain_english: Makino is named as an additional insured on your general liability policy. On your umbrella, they're only covered through a 'whoever is on the underlying is on us' clause that depends on the primary AI endorsement holding up under scrutiny. If a sharp defense attorney challenges the underlying AI status — say, by arguing the operations being claimed against fall outside the CG 20 28 scope — the umbrella drops with the primary. A specifically-scheduled umbrella AI endorsement is bulletproof. Conditional follow-form is good but not bulletproof.
findings.recommendation: Pull the Makino vendor agreement / supply contract. If it requires AI status on umbrella/excess specifically, request that the Umbrella carrier issue a scheduled AI endorsement listing Makino Inc and Black Mountain Aerospace. If Makino's contract only requires AI on 'general liability,' the conditional follow-form is acceptable — but document this analysis for the file.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Umbrella conditional follow-form via CU 00 01 08 22 Section II.6 (Pg. 11) likely covers, subject to underlying AI status
discoveryQuestions: Do you have a copy of the Makino contract or supply agreement that triggers the AI obligation — and what specifically does it require regarding insurance: GL only, or 'all liability coverage including umbrella'?
What's the dollar value and risk profile of the work you do for Makino — does $6M of combined coverage feel sufficient for a worst-case claim, or are they specifying higher limits?
Has Makino ever audited your certificates and pushed back on how they appear on your policies?

findings.requirement_type: Cross-Policy Loss Payee Gap — Wells Fargo Equipment Finance absent from Commercial Auto
findings.contract_quote: N/A — entity matrix evidence: Wells Fargo Equipment Finance Inc, its successors & assigns (MAC S3928-034) appears on BOP only.

findings.gap_description: Wells Fargo Equipment Finance Inc, its successors & assigns is named on the BOP via 481TPR (08-19) (Pg. 12) — typically meaning Wells Fargo finances equipment listed on the property schedule and holds a loss-payable interest. The same lender frequently finances vehicles. If Wells Fargo finances any vehicle on the Auto schedule, the secured interest is unprotected by the Auto policy because no CA 99 44 (Loss Payable) endorsement names Wells Fargo. A total loss on a financed vehicle would leave Wells Fargo's collateral destroyed with no insurance flow-through to satisfy the loan, putting Precision Aero in technical default of the loan covenant requiring insurance loss-payable status.
findings.plain_english: Wells Fargo finances at least some of your equipment — that's why they're on the property policy as a loss payee. If they also finance any of your vehicles, that same protection isn't on the auto policy. A totaled financed truck means the truck is gone, the loan is still owed, and Wells Fargo has no insurance check coming through to satisfy their security interest. That's a loan-document breach on top of the loss.
findings.recommendation: Cross-check Wells Fargo's loan/lease schedule against the vehicle list on the Auto Dec. For each financed or leased vehicle where Wells Fargo holds the lien, add Wells Fargo Equipment Finance Inc as Loss Payee via CA 99 44 (Loss Payable Clause) endorsement on the Auto policy.
discoveryQuestions: Does Wells Fargo Equipment Finance hold loans or leases on any of Precision Aero's vehicles, or only on machinery/equipment scheduled on the property side?

Have you read the loss-payable / insurance covenant language in the Wells Fargo loan documents — does it require Wells Fargo to be loss payee on all collateral, or is it specific to certain equipment?
If a financed vehicle was totaled tomorrow, what's your understanding of how the insurance proceeds would flow — to you, to Wells Fargo, or split?
